author: Fowler
title: Language model compression via task-aware filters for layer-wise distillation
abstract: For compressing large teacher models into small student models, a common strategy is layer-wise distillation, which trains the student to match the teacher’s hidden representations at every intermediate layer. Yet this procedure is challenging: the student, with lower model capacity than the teacher, is frequently under-fitted, and the teacher’s hidden representations include redundant information that the student does not necessarily need for the target task. To overcome these issues, we introduce the proposed method, which applies task-aware filters to align the student and teacher hidden representations at each layer. These filters choose from the hidden representations the knowledge that is useful for the target task, thereby narrowing the knowledge gap between the two models and enabling the student to fit the target task better. We evaluate the proposed method in two scenarios, continual pre-training and fine-tuning, and it demonstrates significant and consistent improvements over existing distillation methods in both scenarios. Code is available at https://github.com/cliang1453/task-aware-distillation.

author: Johnson
title: Reducing Gender Bias in Distilled Language Models through counterfactual swapping of roles
abstract: Large language models produce fluent text, and compression via knowledge distillation makes them usable under limited compute and memory. Yet they often exhibit biases, such as linking male and female genders to occupations that are intended to be gender-neutral. Consequently, knowledge distillation without fairness constraints can carry over or even magnify a teacher's biases into the distilled model. In response, we introduce an approach that trains a fair model during knowledge distillation to mitigate gender disparity in generation. The proposed method alters standard distillation in two ways, using counterfactual swapping of roles: it adjusts teacher probabilities and it augments the training set. We quantify gender polarity across professions in open-ended generations from the resulting distilled and finetuned GPT-2 models, and we find a large drop in gender disparity with only a small loss in utility. Lastly, we note that decreasing gender polarity in generated language does not yield gains in embedding fairness or in downstream classification fairness.

author: Hill
title: Lifelong learning in Minecraft via a hierarchical deep reinforcement learning architecture
abstract: Minecraft, a popular video game, remains an unsolved, high-dimensional lifelong learning problem. We present a lifelong learning system that transfers and reuses knowledge across tasks while efficiently preserving the previously learned knowledge-base. To enable transfer, the system learns reusable skills for solving tasks in Minecraft. These skills are implemented as deep networks and then integrated into a novel hierarchical deep reinforcement learning architecture using two techniques: (1) an array composed of deep skill modules and (2) a novel variation of policy distillation (Rusu et. al. 2015) for learning skills. This distillation procedure allows the proposed architecture to efficiently retain knowledge and thus scale in lifelong learning by accumulating knowledge and packing multiple reusable skills into one distilled network. In sub-domains of Minecraft, the approach exhibits superior performance and lower learning sample complexity compared to the regular Deep Q Network (Mnih et. al. 2015).

author: Walker
title: Meta Learning for Knowledge Distillation: Enabling a BERT Teacher to Adaptively Teach
abstract: We propose a knowledge distillation (KD) method grounded in meta learning that is simple and effective, in contrast to conventional KD that keeps the teacher fixed during training. Within this framework, the teacher network is updated using feedback from the distilled student's performance so it learns to transfer knowledge more effectively (i.e., the teacher learns to teach). We also add a preliminary update step to increase alignment between the inner-learner and the meta-learner in meta learning algorithms that emphasize an improved inner-learner. On various benchmarks, the proposed method can yield significant improvements over traditional KD algorithms and shows reduced sensitivity to student capacity and hyperparameters, facilitating application of KD to different tasks and models.

author: Doyle
title: A recommender system framework based on knowledge distillation
abstract: In modern recommender systems, knowledge distillation has been adopted as a model compression approach that transfers knowledge from a cumbersome teacher model to a compact student model to lower inference time while preserving performance. Most state-of-the-art methods concentrate on making the student closely match the teacher's predictions, yet prediction outputs only partially expose the teacher's knowledge, which limits these approaches. We present a new framework for knowledge distillation in recommender systems, referred to here simply as the proposed method, that lets the student learn both from knowledge latent within the teacher model and from the teacher's predictions. It comprises two components: (1) a component that directly conveys latent knowledge from the teacher model by leveraging "experts" together with a new expert selection strategy, enabling effective distillation of the teacher's vast knowledge into a capacity-limited student; and (2) a component that transfers information revealed by the teacher's prediction while taking into account relaxed ranking orders among items. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed method surpasses state-of-the-art competitors and attains performance comparable to, or even better than, the teacher model while offering faster inference.

author: Rhodes
title: Knowledge distillation for lifelong language learning
abstract: Carrying out lifelong language learning (LLL) over a stream of varied tasks while matching multi-task counterparts without performance degradation is challenging. To tackle this, we introduce the proposed method, a simple yet efficient approach that can be easily integrated into existing LLL architectures to mitigate such degradation. Concretely, when the LLL model faces a new task, a teacher model is first trained on that task, and its knowledge is transferred to the LLL model through knowledge distillation. This enables the LLL model to adapt to the new task while retaining previously learned knowledge. Experiments show that the proposed method consistently improves previous state-of-the-art models, and the degradation relative to multi-task models on LLL tasks is well mitigated for both sequence generation and text classification tasks.

author: Mcclain
title: Transferring Knowledge via Internal Representation Distillation
abstract: Standard practice trains a small student to imitate a large, cumbersome teacher by optimizing on the teacher's output probabilities as soft-labels. Yet when the teacher is considerably large, even when the student very closely matches the soft-labels, its internal representations can still be markedly different, so internal knowledge is not guaranteed to transfer. Such a mismatch can weaken the generalization that the teacher was meant to pass to the student. We propose distilling internal representations from a large model, such as BERT, into its simplified version. We specify two ways to distill these representations and present various algorithms for carrying out the distillation. On datasets from the GLUE benchmark, we consistently show that adding knowledge distillation from internal representations is more powerful than a method that only uses soft-label distillation.

author: Miller
title: Enhancing Spoken Question Answering Accuracy through Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Spoken question answering (SQA) demands comprehensive machine understanding of complex spoken documents, making the task difficult. Automatic speech recognition (ASR) is central to developing QA systems. However, recent work shows that transcripts from ASR are highly noisy, which critically limit machine comprehension on SQA. To tackle this, we introduce a novel distillation framework as the proposed method. Concretely, we design a training strategy that performs knowledge distillation (KD) from spoken documents and their written counterparts. We take a step toward using the language model as a supervision signal by distilling knowledge, with the goal of leading to better student accuracy by reducing misalignment between automatic and manual transcriptions. On the Spoken-SQuAD dataset, experiments demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms several state-of-the-art language models.

author: Henderson
title: Compressing Multi-Model Ensembles with Adversarial Learning
abstract: High-performing deep neural networks often rely on ensembling several base networks. However, the storage needed for many networks and the test-time cost of running them can preclude deployment in applications with large test sets (e.g., ImageNet). We propose to compress a large, complex trained ensemble into a single network by distilling and transferring knowledge from multiple trained deep neural networks (DNNs) into one DNN. To draw diverse knowledge from different trained teacher models, we adopt an adversarial learning scheme in which a block-wise training loss is defined to guide and optimize a predefined student network to recover knowledge present in the teacher models, while simultaneously driving a discriminator network to distinguish teacher versus student features. Using this ensemble transfer with adversarial learning yields three important advantages: (1) the student trained with discriminators to learn the distilled knowledge is optimized more effectively than the original model; (2) fast inference is realized with a single forward pass, while performance even exceeds traditional ensembles formed from multiple original models; and (3) the student network can learn distilled knowledge from a teacher model with arbitrary structures. Extensive experiments on CIFAR-10/100, SVHN, and ImageNet demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method. On ImageNet, a ResNet-50 based implementation achieves top-1/5 21.79%/5.99% val error, which outperforms the original model by 2.06%/1.14%. Code and models can be found at: https://github.com/AaronHeee/MEAL

author: Robinson
title: Optimizing teacher networks to be student-friendly for knowledge distillation
abstract: We introduce a novel knowledge distillation strategy that facilitates transferring dark knowledge from teacher to student. Unlike most existing methods that rely on effective training of student models when a teacher has been pretrained, the proposed method learns teacher models that are student-friendly and therefore more appropriate for knowledge transfer. During optimization and training of a teacher model, it jointly trains student branches so that the teacher develops student-friendly internal representations. Because our approach primarily focuses on training teacher models and the subsequent knowledge distillation step is straightforward, the majority of existing knowledge distillation methods can integrate this technique to improve diverse student models in both accuracy and convergence speed. The proposed algorithm attains outstanding accuracy across several well-known knowledge distillation techniques and many pairings of teacher and student models, including settings with heterogeneous architectures and without prior knowledge of student models when teacher networks are trained.

author: Wagner
title: Self-derived knowledge distillation for natural language processing
abstract: Deep learning has become central to natural language processing (NLP), where many deep learning models deliver remarkable performance across diverse NLP tasks and, in some cases, even outperform humans. These gains are attributed to efficient knowledge representation in deep learning models. Among approaches aimed at learning more efficient representation, knowledge distillation from pretrained deep networks suggests that additional information present in soft target probabilities can be utilized to train other neural networks. We introduce the proposed method, a knowledge distillation approach that uses the training model itself as the provider of soft target probabilities and distills multimode information from the word embedding space located just below the softmax layer. Because of time complexity, the method approximates the soft target probabilities. In experiments, we apply the proposed method to two different and fundamental NLP tasks: language model and neural machine translation. Experimental results show that the proposed method improves performance on the tasks.

author: Johnson
title: Wide Neural Networks and Knowledge Distillation: a transfer risk bound, efficiency with respect to data, and an imperfect teacher
abstract: Advances on the neural tangent kernel indicate that a wide neural network can be approximated by a linear model built from the network's random features. From this perspective, we carry out a theoretical analysis of knowledge distillation in wide neural networks. Knowledge distillation trains a student network using soft output from a teacher network and is widely applied for model compression as well as knowledge transfer, yet a convincing theoretical account is still missing. For the linearized model, we establish a transfer risk bound. We also introduce a metric that quantifies the task’s training difficulty. Using this metric, we show that, with a perfect teacher, allocating a high ratio to the teacher's soft labels can be beneficial. In contrast, when the teacher is imperfect, we find that hard labels can correct the teacher's wrong prediction, which helps explain the common use of a mixture of hard and soft labels.

author: Gonzalez
title: Stepwise knowledge distillation with scratch and expert teachers
abstract: Large storage and compute demands hinder deploying deep neural networks on resource-limited devices. Knowledge distillation trains a compact student network by transferring knowledge from a larger pre-trained teacher model. Yet most approaches overlook informative signals from the training process that are tied to the training results. We present the proposed knowledge distillation strategy that employs two special teachers. One teacher trained from scratch (i.e., scratch teacher) provides step-by-step assistance via its temporary outputs. It forces the student to track an optimal path toward the final logits with high accuracy. The other pre-trained teacher (i.e., expert teacher) guides the student to focus on a critical region that is more useful for the task. Combining knowledge from these two special teachers can significantly improve the student network's performance in knowledge distillation. Results on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, SVHN, and Tiny ImageNet datasets verify efficiency and show state-of-the-art performance for the proposed knowledge distillation method.

author: Santos
title: Knowledge distillation with channel-wise attention, correct-output guidance, and early loss weight decay
abstract: Knowledge distillation conveys what a teacher network has learned from data to a student network, targeting comparable accuracy with fewer parameters and reduced computation. This work presents a new distillation method composed of two transfer strategies and a strategy that decays the loss. The first transfer strategy is built on channel-wise attention and passes channel information from the teacher to the student. The second is a guided scheme that, unlike Knowledge Distillation (KD) which has the student imitate the teacher’s per-sample prediction distribution, restricts imitation to the teacher’s correct output. Finally, during training we progressively reduce the weight on the distillation loss so that the student, rather than the teacher, increasingly drives the optimization. We evaluate on ImageNet and CIFAR100. Using ResNet18 on ImageNet, the top-1 error reaches 27.68%, which outperforms state-of-the-art methods. On CIFAR100, we observe the surprising outcome that the student outperforms the teacher. Code is available at https://github.com/zhouzaida/channel-distillation.

author: Gardner
title: Transferring adversarial robustness from teacher to student via knowledge distillation
abstract: Although knowledge distillation is a strong approach for producing compact, high-performance neural network classifiers, the resulting small models remain vulnerable to adversarial attacks. We investigate how adversarial robustness passes from a teacher to a student under knowledge distillation, and we observe that the student may inherit a large amount of robustness even when trained by distillation solely on clean images. Building on this, we present the proposed method, a procedure that distills robustness into student networks. As with conventional distillation, it yields compact models with high accuracy on the test set, while also conveying the superior robustness of large networks to the student. In experiments, students trained with the proposed method decisively outperform adversarially trained networks of the same architecture in robust accuracy, and they surpass state-of-the-art approaches on standard robustness benchmarks. Finally, we adapt recent fast adversarial training methods to the proposed method to accelerate robust distillation.

author: Robinson
title: Probing ensemble, knowledge distillation, and self-distillation within deep learning
abstract: We present a formal analysis of when and why ensemble of deep learning models can raise test accuracy, and how the superior performance of an ensemble can be distilled into one model via knowledge distillation. Our focus is the particularly challenging setting where the ensemble is the average of the outputs of a few neural networks trained independently that share the SAME architecture, use the SAME algorithm, operate on the SAME data set, and differ only in the random seeds at initialization. We show that ensemble/knowledge distillation in Deep Learning behaves very differently than what traditional learning theory predicts (e.g., boosting or neural tangent kernels (NTKs)). To explain these phenomena, we develop a theory establishing that, when the data exhibit a structure we call "multi-view", an ensemble of such independently trained neural networks can provably improve test accuracy, and this superior test accuracy can also be provably distilled into a single model by training it to match the output of the ensemble rather than the true label. These results clarify that ensemble in deep learning functions in a manner completely unlike classical theorems, and that "dark knowledge" resides in the outputs of the ensemble and is usable for distillation. Finally, we prove that self-distillation can also be understood as implicitly combining ensemble and knowledge distillation to improve test accuracy.

author: Lawrence
title: Distillation from a Deep Pose Regression Teacher
abstract: In pose regression for Visual Odometry (VO), conventional distillation hinges on "dark knowledge" for successful transfer, which is absent in this setting, and the teacher prediction may be unreliable. We therefore transfer knowledge only when the teacher is trusted: the teacher loss is treated as a confidence score that adaptively scales the relative weight given to the teacher prediction. This confidence gates both the main training objective through an attention-weighted imitation loss and the learning of the teacher’s intermediate representation through an attention-weighted hint training procedure. Using this design, we distill knowledge from a deep pose regressor network to obtain a more efficient VO student. To the best of the authors' knowledge, this is the first work that successfully distills knowledge from a deep pose regressor network. On the KITTI and Malaga datasets, our evaluation shows the student remains close to the teacher while achieving up to a 92.95% reduction in parameters and a 2.12x speedup in computation time.

author: Pacheco
title: Distilling Knowledge Using Adversarial Samples that Support the Decision Boundary
abstract: Selecting an effective technique for knowledge distillation remains open, even though numerous recent studies have shown how to transfer the knowledge of a trained network to accelerate the learning of a new one. We approach this issue by centering the analysis on the decision boundary, a key component of any classifier. Because the generalization performance of a classifier is tightly linked to how adequate its decision boundary is, a good classifier necessarily possesses a good decision boundary. This observation suggests that passing information that is tightly associated with the decision boundary is a promising way to conduct knowledge distillation. To operationalize this idea, we apply an adversarial attack to identify samples that support a decision boundary. Using these samples, the proposed method trains a student classifier so that more accurate information about the decision boundary is transferred. Experimental results confirm that the proposed method indeed improves knowledge distillation and attains state-of-the-art performance.

author: Smith
title: Understanding knowledge distillation via quantification of knowledge
abstract: We propose an approach to interpret why knowledge distillation succeeds by quantifying and analyzing visual concepts—both task-relevant and task-irrelevant—encoded within a deep neural network (DNN)’s intermediate layers. To assess feature representations, we construct three types of mathematical metrics. The work advances three hypotheses: (1) compared with learning from raw data, knowledge distillation leads the DNN to learn more visual concepts; (2) knowledge distillation ensures the DNN is prone to simultaneously learning diverse visual concepts, whereas when trained on raw data the DNN acquires visual concepts sequentially; and (3) relative to learning from raw data, knowledge distillation produces more stable optimization directions. In experiments, we conducted diagnoses on various DNNs, and the above hypotheses were verified.

author: Shaffer
title: Sample Selection for Knowledge Distillation in Neural Machine Translation
abstract: Neural Machine Translation (NMT) models set the state of the art on many translation benchmarks. In NMT, knowledge distillation has become an active line of work and is commonly used to boost performance by transferring a teacher model's knowledge on each training sample. Yet prior studies seldom analyze how individual samples differ in impact or how they relate to one another, even though these samples act as the medium through which teacher knowledge is transferred. We introduce a new protocol that effectively examines sample impact by contrasting multiple partitions of the sample set. Using this protocol, we conduct extensive experiments and observe that adding more teacher knowledge is not invariably beneficial; for certain samples, transferring knowledge may even degrade the overall performance of knowledge distillation. To cope with these issues, we present two simple but effective selection strategies—batch-level and global-level—to choose appropriate samples for distillation. We assess the proposed approach on two large-scale machine translation tasks, WMT'14 English->German and WMT'19 Chinese->English. The results show improvements of up to +1.28 and +0.89 BLEU points over the Transformer baseline on these two tasks, respectively.

author: Wolfe
title: Robust, Resource-Efficient Data-Free Knowledge Distillation via VAE-Based Synthetic Replay
abstract: In Data-Free Knowledge Distillation (KD), a trained neural network (teacher) transfers knowledge to a smaller student without access to the original training set. Many approaches track student accuracy on real data using a validation set and then report the best value reached at any time during distillation. However, a validation set may also be absent at distillation time, making it impossible to select the student snapshot that attained the peak accuracy. Consequently, a practical data-free KD procedure ought to be robust and, ideally, yield a monotonic rise in student accuracy as distillation proceeds. Achieving this is difficult since distribution shift in the synthetic data causes knowledge degradation in the student. A direct remedy is to cache generated samples and rehearse them periodically, but doing so inflates memory usage and raises privacy concerns. We instead fit a generative network to the distribution of synthetic samples observed earlier. Concretely, we construct a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) and tailor its training objective to optimally capture representations of the synthetic data. During distillation, the student is rehearsed using samples drawn from this VAE, which acts as a generator to replay prior synthetic content. This prevents knowledge degradation while storing no samples. Experiments on image classification benchmarks indicate that the proposed method optimizes the expected value of the distilled model accuracy while eliminating the large memory overhead incurred by the sample-storing methods.

author: Peterson
title: Probing why knowledge distillation benefits non-autoregressive machine translation
abstract: Knowledge distillation is widely used for non-autoregressive machine translation (NAT) and, empirically, yields large accuracy improvements for NAT models, yet why it is crucial has remained unclear. We perform systematic experiments to analyze this phenomenon. Our analysis shows that knowledge distillation reduces the complexity of data sets and enables NAT to model variations in the output data. We further identify a strong correlation linking an NAT model’s capacity to the distilled data’s optimal complexity for attaining the best translation quality. Guided by these observations, we introduce several approaches that modify data set complexity to improve the performance of NAT models. As a result, we obtain state-of-the-art results among NAT-based models and close the gap to the autoregressive baseline on the WMT14 En-De benchmark. For context, in NAT the system predicts output tokens in parallel across the sequence, delivering substantial gains in generation speed over autoregressive models. Moreover, existing NAT models usually rely on knowledge distillation, which constructs the training data using a pretrained autoregressive model, to achieve better performance.

author: Moore
title: Attention-based matching of features for knowledge distillation
abstract: In knowledge distillation, a pre-trained teacher network conveys general knowledge to a target student network. A common practice is to create manual ties between intermediate features in the teacher and the student and to transfer knowledge through pre-defined links. Such manual selection frequently forms ineffective links that cap the improvement achievable from the distillation. Although there has been an attempt to address this issue, selecting effective links under practical scenarios remains challenging. We present an effective and efficient feature distillation approach that uses all feature levels from the teacher while avoiding any manual choice of links. The proposed method employs an attention-based meta-network to learn relative similarities between features and then uses the learned similarities to control distillation intensities for all possible pairs. As a consequence, it finds competent links with higher efficiency than the previous approach, and it yields better performance on transfer learning tasks and model compression. Ablative studies and qualitative analyses further describe how the method contributes to better distillation. Code is available at github.com/clovaai/attention-feature-distillation.

author: Bernard
title: Reinforcement-based dynamic multi-teacher weighting for knowledge distillation
abstract: For tasks in natural language processing (NLP), slow inference and large GPU memory footprints still constitute the bottleneck to applying pre-trained deep models in production. As a popular model compression technique, knowledge distillation passes knowledge from one or more large (teacher) models to a small (student) model. When multiple teacher models are used, state-of-the-art methods typically keep a fixed weight for each teacher throughout the entire distillation process. Moreover, most existing methods give every teacher model the same weight. We observe that, because training examples vary in complexity and student model capability differs, learning differentially from teacher models can yield better performance for distilled student models. Accordingly, we systematically construct a reinforced method that dynamically assigns weights to teacher models on a per-instance basis to optimize student model performance. A large set of experiments across several NLP tasks provides clear evidence for the feasibility and effectiveness of the approach.

author: Rogers
title: Ground-Truth-Guided Weighting for Multi-Teacher Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Historically, knowledge distillation trained a student with auxiliary supervision from a single teacher. To raise student performance, more recent variants draw on multiple teachers to harvest diverse knowledge. Yet many prior studies fuse these sources by averaging teacher predictions or by other label-free aggregation, which can steer the student incorrectly when some teachers produce low-quality predictions. We address this by proposing a method that, with ground-truth labels, adaptively assigns sample-wise reliability to each teacher prediction, giving larger weights to predictions that are closer to one-hot labels. In addition, the approach leverages intermediate layers to stabilize the knowledge transfer process. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed method consistently outperforms every state-of-the-art method in the comparison across various teacher-student architectures.

author: Davis
title: Adversarial online knowledge distillation using feature maps
abstract: Feature maps encode rich cues about image intensity and spatial correlation. Nevertheless, most online knowledge distillation techniques have relied solely on the class probabilities. We present an online knowledge distillation approach that conveys both the class probabilities and feature map knowledge via an adversarial training framework. We simultaneously train multiple networks and use discriminators to separate the feature map distributions across networks. Each network is paired with a discriminator that marks its own feature map as fake while deeming that from the other network real. By learning to fool its discriminator, a network aligns to the other network's feature map distribution. We show that, relative to conventional direct alignment (e.g., L1), our method performs better and is more suitable for online distillation. We also introduce a novel cyclic learning scheme to train more than two networks simultaneously. Applied across various network architectures for the classification task, the approach yields significant performance improvement, with especially notable gains when a small network is trained together with a large one as a pair.

author: Abbott
title: Adversarial knowledge distillation for compact deep graph neural networks
abstract: Deep graph neural networks (GNNs) exhibit strong expressiveness when modeling graph-structured data. Yet, their over-stacked architectures make deployment and rapid testing on mobile and embedded systems difficult. A common way to compress such over-stacked GNNs is to perform knowledge distillation using a teacher-student architecture; the central operation is quantifying the discrepancy between teacher and student with predefined distance functions. However, a single distance across graphs with diverse structures can be ill-suited, and identifying an optimal distance formulation is difficult. To address this, the proposed method adopts adversarial knowledge distillation for graph models by jointly training a discriminator and a generator to adaptively detect and reduce the discrepancy. Motivated by the role of well-captured inter-node and inter-class correlations in the success of deep GNNs, we scrutinize the inherited knowledge at node-level and class-level through a trainable discriminator. The discriminator separates teacher knowledge from what the student inherits, and the student GNN acts as the generator that tries to fool it. To our best knowledge, the proposed method is the first to introduce adversarial training into knowledge distillation for graph domains. Experiments on node-level and graph-level classification benchmarks show that the proposed method improves the performance of the student by a large margin. These results imply that the proposed method can precisely transfer knowledge from a complicated teacher GNN to a compact student GNN.

author: Munoz
title: Distilling Knowledge in Deep Networks Without Training Data
abstract: In knowledge distillation, a compact Student is trained to imitate a high-capacity Teacher so that most of the Teacher’s performance is preserved. Prior approaches typically rely on the original training data or on meta-data derived from it to optimize the Student. Yet the dataset used to train the Teacher can be inaccessible when it is extremely large or when privacy or safety issues arise (e.g., bio-metric or medical data). To address this, we put forward a data-free procedure that trains the Student directly from the Teacher. With no meta-data at all, we synthesize inputs from the complex Teacher model and employ these as substitutes for the original training data samples, thereby conveying its learning to the Student through knowledge distillation. We refer to this approach simply as the proposed method, and we demonstrate that the resulting framework yields generalization performance competitive with distillation that uses the actual training data samples on multiple benchmark datasets.

author: Roman
title: Advancing Fairness in Visual Recognition via Feature Distillation
abstract: In computer vision, and particularly in systems that render decisions about people, concerns about fairness have grown in importance. Yet obtaining algorithmic fairness—so that a model yields outcomes that do not discriminate against protected groups—remains unresolved. We present a systematic feature distillation strategy for visual recognition that reduces algorithmic biases; it leverages MMD and will be referred to here simply as the proposed method. Although distillation has been widely applied to boost prediction accuracy, to our knowledge there is no explicit prior work that also aims to improve fairness via distillation. In addition, we provide a theoretical justification for the proposed method concerning the effect of knowledge distillation and fairness. Through extensive experiments, we show the proposed method significantly mitigates bias against specific minorities, without any loss in accuracy, on synthetic as well as real-world face datasets.

author: Blair
title: A systematic study of policy distillation
abstract: In Deep Reinforcement Learning, transferring knowledge from a policy to another policy is a key mechanism. This mechanism, termed distillation, has been shown to be highly effective; for example, it improves the optimisation of agents, leading to faster and stronger performance on harder domains [26, 32, 5, 8]. Nevertheless, despite its simple idea and widespread adoption, practitioners employ many formulations of distillation, and small design changes can markedly shift both the optimised objective and the resulting performance. We present a rigorous, comprehensive examination of policy distillation, assessing the motivations and strengths of each variant via theoretical and empirical analysis. Our findings indicate three distillation techniques that are preferable depending on task specifics. In particular, the proposed method, which uses expected entropy regularisation within distillation, allows for quicker learning across a wide range of situations while still guaranteeing convergence.

author: Herrera
title: Distilling Object Detectors by imitating teacher features at estimated near-object anchor locations
abstract: Many state-of-the-art CNN-based recognition models are too computationally demanding for low-end devices. Knowledge distillation, which has a small student model imitate a cumbersome teacher model’s outputs to improve generalization, is a promising high-level strategy, but prior work has mainly targeted the simpler classification setting rather than complex tasks such as object detection. We show that applying vanilla knowledge distillation to a detection model yields only minor gains. To tackle the challenge of distillation for detection, we introduce a method that exploits the cross-location discrepancy in the feature response. The central intuition is that detectors emphasize local regions near objects; therefore, differences in feature response at near object anchor locations expose important signals about how the teacher model tends to generalize. We design a novel mechanism to estimate these locations and have the student model imitate the teacher there to enhance performance. We first validate this idea on a lightweight toy detector that captures the simplest notion of current state-of-the-art anchor-based detection models on the challenging KITTI dataset, where the approach delivers up to a 15% boost in mAP for the student model compared to a non-imitated counterpart. We then extensively evaluate with a Faster R-CNN model under various scenarios on the common object detection benchmarks Pascal VOC and COCO, where imitation alleviates up to 74% of the performance drop of the student model relative to the teacher. Codes released at https://github.com/twangnh/Distilling-Object-Detectors

author: Dudley
title: Answer Distillation with Ensemble-Guided Alignment for Machine Reading Comprehension
abstract: Progress in reading comprehension systems has been substantial, yet the strongest results typically require an ensemble of many models, and these approaches remain vulnerable to adversarial attacks. We address both issues using knowledge distillation, whose aim is to transfer knowledge from an ensemble to a single model. As a first step, we show that, for answer span prediction, vanilla knowledge distillation is effective in reading comprehension systems. Building on this, we introduce two novel approaches that (i) penalize predictions on confusing answers and (ii) guide training with alignment information that is distilled from the ensemble. In experiments, our best student model exhibits only a slight 0.4% F1 drop on the SQuAD test set relative to the ensemble teacher, while running 12x faster at inference. It even outperforms the teacher on the adversarial SQuAD datasets and the NarrativeQA benchmark.

author: Gray
title: Progressive Replacement of Modules for BERT Compression
abstract: We introduce a novel method that effectively compresses BERT by progressively replacing modules. The proposed method partitions the original BERT into multiple modules, constructs compact substitutes for each, and trains these compact modules to mimic their originals by randomly swapping substitutes in place of the originals during learning. The replacement probability is increased over the course of training, which produces a deeper level of interaction between the compact and original models. Unlike earlier knowledge distillation approaches to BERT compression, no additional loss function is required. On the GLUE benchmark, the method outperforms existing knowledge distillation approaches, offering a different perspective on model compression.

author: Arnold
title: Is Knowledge Distillation Effective?
abstract: Using knowledge distillation to train a small student network to imitate a larger teacher model, such as an ensemble of networks, is widely practiced. We find that, although knowledge distillation can improve student generalization, it does not typically operate as commonly assumed: even in settings where the student has the capacity to match the teacher perfectly, a surprisingly large discrepancy often remains between the teacher's and student's predictive distributions. We point to difficulties in optimization as a key reason the student fails to match the teacher. We also demonstrate that properties of the dataset used for distillation affect how closely the student matches the teacher, and that, paradoxically, achieving a closer match to the teacher does not always yield better student generalization.

author: Calderon
title: Knowledge distillation for generalizable neural solvers of vehicle routing problems
abstract: Existing neural approaches to vehicle routing problems have always trained and tested deep models under a single instance distribution (uniform), and this raises concerns about cross-distribution generalization. To confront this issue, we introduce knowledge distillation into this domain and develop the proposed method: an adaptive scheme that performs distillation across multiple exemplar distributions to learn more generalizable deep models. Specifically, multiple teachers trained on exemplar distributions contribute complementary knowledge that is integrated to obtain a student model that is light-weight yet generalist. An adaptive strategy further directs the student’s attention toward difficult distributions, enabling more effective acquisition of hard-to-master knowledge. Extensive experimental results show that, compared with baseline neural methods, the proposed method is able to deliver competitive performance on unseen instances from both the in-distribution and out-of-distribution, whether randomly synthesized or drawn from benchmark datasets (i.e., TSPLIB and CVRPLIB). Notably, the approach is generic and consumes less computational resources for inference.

author: Montgomery
title: 3D Object Detection on Point Clouds via Dynamic Graph Message Passing
abstract: Pipelines for training and testing 3D object detection are often intricate and tied to dataset-specific expertise. Motivated by 2D object detectors that do not use non-maximum suppression, we present a 3D point-cloud architecture. The proposed method formulates detection as passing messages across a dynamic graph and extends the DGCNN framework so it predicts a set of objects. With this design, post-processing via object confidence aggregation or non-maximum suppression is unnecessary. To better handle sparse point clouds, we further introduce a set-to-set distillation strategy tailored to 3D detection. This strategy aligns teacher model and student model outputs in a permutation-invariant way, thereby significantly simplifying knowledge distillation for 3D detection. On autonomous driving benchmarks, the method attains state-of-the-art performance. We also provide substantial analysis of the detector and the distillation framework.

author: Hensley
title: Improving Accuracy of Low-Precision Networks via Knowledge Distillation Techniques
abstract: Deep learning networks currently deliver state-of-the-art accuracies on computer vision tasks, including image classification and object detection. Yet the highest-performing systems generally depend on large models with many parameters. After training, deploying such top performing models to resource-constrained inference platforms is difficult because these models—often deep networks, wide networks, or both—are compute- and memory-intensive. Low-precision numerics and model compression using knowledge distillation are popular techniques to reduce both compute requirements and memory footprint for deployed models. We investigate combining these two techniques and demonstrate that the performance of low-precision networks can be significantly improved by applying knowledge distillation techniques. The proposed method attains state-of-the-art accuracies with ternary precision and 4-bit precision on variants of the ResNet architecture evaluated on the ImageNet dataset. We describe three schemes that apply knowledge distillation techniques at different stages of the training-and-deployment pipeline.

author: Ray
title: Conveying inductive biases by means of knowledge distillation
abstract: We examine the ability of knowledge distillation to carry over the influence of inductive biases from one model to a different model. This question matters in tasks and scenarios with scarce data or constrained computation, or when the training set does not accurately reflect test-time conditions. Specifying, designing, and efficiently adapting inductive biases is often nontrivial, motivating our study. We analyze families of architectures that embody distinct inductive biases—contrasting LSTMs with Transformers, and CNNs with MLPs—within settings where the choice of inductive biases is crucial. We characterize how these inductive biases shape the solutions to which models converge, and we probe, through knowledge distillation, the extent and manner in which their influence is conveyed, evaluating not only performance but also multiple facets of the converged solutions.

author: Bush
title: Leveraging Knowledge Distillation from Weakly-Supervised Detection to Improve Multi-Label Image Classification
abstract: A core yet difficult problem for general visual understanding is multi-label image classification. Prior work has shown that region-level information (e.g., features from RoIs) benefits this task. But such approaches typically rely on laborious object-level annotations (i.e., bounding boxes and object labels) to learn object-level visual features effectively. We present a novel and efficient deep framework that improves multi-label classification by distilling knowledge from a weakly-supervised detection task, while requiring no bounding box annotations. With only image-level annotations available, we first train a weakly-supervised detection (WSD) model and then build an end-to-end framework for multi-label image classification equipped with a knowledge distillation module. This module transfers guidance from the WSD teacher to the classification student using both class-level predictions for the whole image and object-level visual features for object RoIs. Through distillation across tasks, the classification model attains significantly improved performance, and efficiency is preserved because the WSD model can be discarded during testing. Extensive experiments on two large-scale datasets, MS-COCO and NUS-WIDE, show that the proposed method achieves superior performances relative to state-of-the-art methods on both performance and efficiency.

author: Williams
title: Relational Distillation for Link Prediction with MLPs
abstract: On link prediction, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are strong performers; however, latency arising from complex neighborhood dependencies hinders practical use. By contrast, efficient MLPs lag behind GNNs owing to missing relational knowledge. To couple the strengths of GNNs and MLPs, we first assess straightforward knowledge distillation (KD) variants for link prediction: matching predicted logits and matching node representations. After finding that such direct KD analogs underperform on link prediction, we introduce the proposed method, a relational KD framework that transfers knowledge for link prediction to MLPs. Rather than aligning link logits treated as independent, or standalone node representations, the proposed method conveys relational knowledge organized around each (anchor) node to the student MLP. It employs complementary rank-based matching and distribution-based matching strategies. Comprehensive experiments show that the proposed method lifts MLP link prediction by significant margins, and even exceeds the teacher GNNs on 7 of 8 benchmarks overall. It also delivers a 70.68x speedup in link prediction inference relative to GNNs on the large-scale OGB dataset.

author: Perez
title: Unsupervised domain adaptation from single or multiple black-box predictors
abstract: This paper studies a practical and interesting setting for UDA in which, during adaptation on the target domain, only black-box source models are accessible (i.e., only the network predictions are available). To ease the burden of labeling, the goal in UDA is to exploit earlier, related labeled datasets (sources) to benefit a new unlabeled dataset (target). Many prior approaches presume access to the raw source data and design data-dependent alignment procedures to recognize target samples in a transductive learning setting, raising privacy concerns from source individuals. A separate line of recent work instead uses a well-trained white-box source model, yet generative adversarial learning can still leak raw data. To tackle the black-box scenario, the proposed method employs a two-step knowledge adaptation framework. Accounting for the structure of the target data, it first distills knowledge from the source predictor into a customized target model, and then fine-tunes the distilled model, further fitting the target domain. Neural networks across domains need not be identical in the proposed method, which even allows effective adaptation on a low-resource device. Experiments on three UDA scenarios—single-source, multi-source, and partial-set—show that the proposed method yields highly competitive performance relative to state-of-the-art data-dependent approaches. Code is available at https://github.com/tim-learn/DINE/.

author: Roberts
title: Achieving Interpretability in Deep Neural Networks through Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Although Deep Neural Networks have shown strong performance across a wide spectrum of applications, spanning computer vision, language modeling, and speech recognition, practical deployment often requires interpretability, especially in ethically sensitive and mission critical applications. The complexity of these models makes predictions difficult to understand and reason about, which hinders further progress. To address this need, the proposed method uses Knowledge Distillation to distill Deep Neural Networks to decision trees so that interpretability and good performance are obtained simultaneously. We pose the task as a multi-output regression problem. In experiments, under the same level of tree depth, the student model attains performance in accuracy that is significantly better (about 1% to 5%) than vanilla decision trees. We implement the experiments on the TensorFlow platform, which makes it scalable to big datasets. As far as we are aware, no prior work has distilled Deep Neural Networks to vanilla decision trees on multi-class datasets.

author: Miller
title: Probing BERT Rankers via Distillation
abstract: Pre-trained deep language models like BERT, trained on a large corpus, have given a huge performance boost to ranking systems for information retrieval that represent the state of the art. The knowledge encoded in these models enables detection of complex matching signals between queries and passages. Nevertheless, high computation cost at inference limits their use in real-world search scenarios. We investigate whether, and in what way, the search knowledge inside BERT can be transferred to a smaller ranker via distillation. Our experiments show that employing a proper distillation procedure is crucial, yielding up to nine times speedup while preserving state-of-the-art performance.

author: Hall
title: Zero-shot knowledge transfer for federated learning under resource constraints with heterogeneous on-device models
abstract: In federated learning, a set of distributed devices jointly trains a shared prediction model while keeping their on-device data decentralized. However, many existing algorithms presume comparable per-device effort for local training and identical structure and size of on-device models, which hinders participation by resource-constrained devices. To address increasingly widespread yet heterogeneous devices, we introduce a federated learning framework that supports heterogeneous on-device models via zero-shot knowledge transfer (the proposed method). Concretely, the proposed method lets each device choose its on-device model according to its local resources. To enable knowledge transfer among these heterogeneous on-device models, we design a zero-shot distillation approach that has no prerequisites for private on-device data, in contrast to prior work that depends on a public dataset or a pre-trained data generator. Furthermore, to make participation feasible for resource-constrained devices, the compute-intensive distillation is carried out on the server, where a generator is adversarially learned with the ensemble of collected on-device models. The server then returns the distilled central knowledge as the corresponding on-device model parameters, which can be readily absorbed on the device side. Extensive experimental studies demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed method with respect to on-device knowledge agnostic, on-device model heterogeneity, and other challenging federated learning scenarios, such as heterogeneous on-device data and straggler effects.

author: Garcia
title: Knowledge Distillation for a Compact Visual-linguistic Model
abstract: Using the proposed distillation, a small VL model reaches 120.8 CIDEr on COCO captioning, improving its non-distilled counterpart by 5.1, and attains 69.8 accuracy on VQA 2.0, a 0.8 gain over the baseline. Extensive experiments and ablations confirm that VL distillation is effective during both the pre-training and fine-tuning stages. We investigate knowledge distillation (KD) as a means to compress a transformer-based large VL model, producing a small VL model, since compact models remain scarce even with rapid progress in pre-training for visual-linguistic (VL) representations. A central obstacle is that the Teacher and Student rely on different detectors; the resulting regional visual tokens are inconsistent, which misaligns hidden representations and attention distributions. To overcome this, we retrain and adapt the Teacher to take the same region proposals from the Student's detector while retaining features from the Teacher's own object detector. Once the network inputs are aligned, the adapted Teacher can transfer knowledge via intermediate representations. Concretely, we apply a mean square error loss to approximate the attention distribution within the transformer block, and we introduce a token-wise noise contrastive loss that aligns the hidden state by contrasting against negative representations kept in a sample queue. These elements together significantly improve small VL models on the tasks of image captioning and visual question answering.

author: Ramirez
title: Regularization with progressively softened targets via self-distillation
abstract: Generalization in deep neural networks has been substantially improved through a broad spectrum of regularization methods, e.g., augmenting data, restricting function space, injecting randomness during training, etc. We introduce a simple yet effective regularization approach that, during training, performs progressive distillation of the model’s own knowledge so that hard targets (i.e., one-hot vectors) are softened. In the framework of knowledge distillation, the student effectively serves as its own teacher. Concretely, the targets are adapted on the fly by combining the ground-truth with the model’s past predictions. We show that the proposed method yields an effect of hard example mining by rescaling gradients in proportion to the difficulty of classifying examples. The approach applies to any supervised learning task that uses hard targets and can be readily paired with existing regularization methods to further enhance generalization performance. Furthermore, it is confirmed that the proposed method achieves not only better accuracy, but also provides high quality confidence estimates in terms of calibration as well as ordinal ranking. Extensive experiments across three different tasks—machine translation, image classification, and object detection—demonstrate that our method consistently improves the performance of state-of-the-art baselines. Code is available at https://github.com/lgcnsai/PS-KD-Pytorch.

author: Reid
title: Distillation with Low-Cost Convolutions
abstract: Deploying modern neural networks on tight memory budgets is widely desired, but flexible techniques to cut memory remain nascent, and the resulting trade-offs are not well quantified. We present the proposed method, a distillation approach targeted at memory reduction in which the student architecture is obtained via a straightforward transform of the teacher architecture; it requires no redesign, and identical hyperparameters can be reused. Using attention transfer, we provide Pareto fronts and tabulations when distilling residual networks on four benchmark datasets, characterizing the accuracy–memory payoff. We show that substantial memory savings are feasible with very little loss in accuracy, and we also confirm that distillation gives student network performance that is better than training the student architecture directly on data.

author: Diaz
title: Compressing Models for a Web Question Answering System using a Two-Stage Multi-Teacher Knowledge Distillation Method
abstract: Pre-training and fine-tuning with large models such as BERT and OpenAI GPT yield excellent performance on question answering, but the very large number of parameters makes inference speed very slow, which complicates using these complex models in real business scenarios. Model compression has been explored, yet typical model compression methods suffer from information loss during the model compression procedure and therefore produce models inferior to the original one. To address this, the proposed method applies a two-stage multi-teacher knowledge distillation strategy for a web Question Answering system. First, we construct a general Q&A distillation task to pre-train a student model. Then, we fine-tune this pre-trained student with multi-teacher knowledge distillation on downstream tasks, including the Web Q&A task and MNLI, SNLI, and RTE from GLUE. This two-step process effectively reduces the overfitting bias present in individual teacher models and transfers more general knowledge to the student model. Experimental results indicate that the method can significantly outperform the baseline methods and even achieve results comparable to the original teacher models, while also delivering a substantial acceleration in model inference.

author: Wood
title: Identifying Effective Data Augmentation for Knowledge Distillation: A Statistical Viewpoint
abstract: In knowledge distillation (KD), a teacher model steers the training of a student model and serves as a general neural network training approach. Prior studies have focused primarily on the network output side (e.g., devising improved KD loss functions), with comparatively few efforts to analyze the input side; in particular, how KD interacts with data augmentation (DA) remains insufficiently understood. We pose two questions: why do some DA schemes, such as CutMix, inherently achieve much better KD performance than others, and what characterizes a "good" DA for KD? From a statistical analysis, we find that an effective DA should reduce the covariance of the teacher-student cross-entropy. We further introduce a practical metric, the stddev of the teacher's mean probability (T. stddev), and show that it is well justified empirically. Beyond this theoretical understanding, we also present a new entropy-based data-mixing DA scheme intended to enhance CutMix; the proposed method serves this role. Extensive empirical studies support these claims and demonstrate that simply adopting a better DA scheme in knowledge distillation can yield considerable performance gains.

author: Clark
title: A Knowledge Distillation Method for Ultra-Resolution Universal Style Transfer
abstract: Universal style transfer commonly relies on rich features from deep Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) models such as VGG-19 pre-trained on large-scale image collections; however, memory constraints make executing these large models on ultra-resolution images challenging. We propose a new knowledge distillation method for encoder-decoder–based neural style transfer to reduce the convolutional filters. The approach is motivated by the observation that encoder-decoder pairs form an exclusive collaborative relationship, which we treat as a new kind of knowledge for style transfer models. To address feature size mismatch during application of the proposed method, we introduce a linear embedding loss so that the student network learns a linear embedding of the features from the teacher. Extensive experiments demonstrate effectiveness when the method is applied to WCT and AdaIN, two universal style transfer approaches, despite a 15.5 times reduction in model size. In particular, with compressed models on WCT, we perform, for the first time, universal style transfer at ultra-resolution (over 40 megapixels) on a 12GB GPU. Further experiments on an optimization-based stylization scheme show the generality of our algorithm across different stylization paradigms. Code and trained models are available at https://github.com/mingsun-tse/collaborative-distillation.

author: Adams
title: Re-examining heuristics for deep learning: distillation, warmup, and learning rate restarts
abstract: Widely used deep learning models attain faster convergence and better final performance in large part due to heuristics such as skip connections, normalization layers, learning rate schedules, and knowledge distillation. In the continuing absence of strong theoretical underpinnings, controlled experiments designed to explain these strategies can sharpen our understanding of deep learning landscapes and training dynamics. Empirical analyses have often used visualizations with dimensionality reduction and linear interpolation, but each comes with limitations. We instead revisit these heuristics using recently introduced tools for representation and loss surface analysis—canonical correlation analysis (CCA) and mode connectivity—and propose hypotheses for their success. Specifically, we study knowledge distillation and learning rate heuristics of (cosine) restarts and warmup via mode connectivity and CCA. Our empirical analysis suggests that: (a) commonly cited explanations for the success of cosine annealing do not appear in practice; (b) learning rate warmup serves to keep the deeper layers from inducing training instability; and (c) the latent knowledge shared by the teacher is primarily transferred to the deeper layers.

author: Zuniga
title: Scaling distributed neural network training via an online form of distillation
abstract: We first show that an online variant of distillation can exploit extra parallelism to fit very large datasets about twice as fast. Crucially, the speedup persists even beyond the point where adding more parallelism ceases to help stochastic gradient descent, whether synchronous or asynchronous. The mechanism trains two neural networks on disjoint subsets of the data and shares knowledge by encouraging each model to align with the predictions the other would have produced. These predictions may be drawn from a stale version of the peer, allowing them to be computed safely using weights that are transmitted only infrequently. Our second claim is that online distillation offers a cost-effective strategy to make the exact predictions of a model dramatically more reproducible. While ensembling and distillation are known to offer model quality improvements with almost any base model, ensembles raise test-time cost and conventional distillation increases training pipeline complexity, making both difficult to deploy in industrial settings. In contrast, the approach we investigate is relatively simple to adopt, as it avoids a complicated multi-stage setup and does not introduce many new hyperparameters. We support these claims with experiments on the Criteo Display Ad Challenge dataset, on ImageNet, and on the largest to-date dataset for neural language modeling, comprising 6×10^11 tokens derived from the Common Crawl web repository.

author: Wong
title: Domain generalization through knowledge distillation and gradient-filter regularization
abstract: Convolutional neural networks are common across many tasks, yet their generalization capability suffers when sufficient and representative data are unavailable, which limits practical deployment. This work introduces a simple, effective, plug-and-play training strategy, referred to here as the proposed method, that builds on a knowledge distillation framework and incorporates a gradient filter as a new regularization term. We observe that the richer dark knowledge provided by the teacher network, together with the introduced gradient filter, lowers the difficulty involved in learning the mapping and in turn improves the model’s generalization ability. Extensive experiments indicate that this framework can significantly enhance the generalization capability of deep neural networks on diverse tasks—image classification, segmentation, and reinforcement learning—when our method is compared with state-of-the-art techniques for domain generalization. Finally, we adopt two metrics to analyze the proposed method in order to better understand how it benefits the generalization capability of deep neural networks.

author: Lynch
title: Understanding Knowledge Distillation through Label Smoothing Regularization
abstract: Knowledge Distillation (KD) transfers what a high-capacity teacher has learned to a compact student. Its effectiveness is usually attributed to the teacher’s privileged information about inter-class similarity, so in practice only strong teacher models are used to supervise weaker students. We challenge this view with two experimental observations: 1) beyond the fact that a teacher can improve a student, reversing KD so that the student teaches the teacher can significantly enhance the teacher; 2) a poorly trained teacher with much lower accuracy than the student can still improve the student significantly. To account for these findings, we present a theoretical analysis of the relationship between KD and label smoothing regularization, and we prove that 1) KD is a learned form of label smoothing regularization, and 2) label smoothing regularization yields a virtual teacher model for KD. From these results, we argue that the success of KD is not fully due to similarity information between categories from teachers; the regularization effect of soft targets is equally or even more important. Building on this perspective, we introduce a novel proposed method in which a student learns from itself or from a manually designed regularization distribution, without relying on any teacher. This approach achieves performance comparable to normal KD from a superior teacher and is suitable when a stronger teacher model is unavailable. It is generic and can be directly deployed for training deep neural networks. Without any extra computation cost, the proposed method attains up to 0.65% improvement on ImageNet over well-established baseline models, and it is superior to label smoothing regularization.

author: Jackson
title: Online Knowledge Distillation with Contrastive Distribution Exchange for Visual Recognition
abstract: In teacher-free online Knowledge Distillation (KD), multiple student models are trained jointly as an ensemble and distill knowledge from one another. While prior online KD methods achieve strong results, they typically emphasize class probabilities as the principal knowledge signal and neglect feature representational information. We introduce the proposed method, a contrastive, online framework for KD in which a set of networks exchange contrastive distributions with mutual interaction. By pooling cross-network embedding information and maximizing a mutual-information lower bound between pairs of networks, the method encourages each network to acquire additional contrastive knowledge from its peers. This improves feature representations and, in turn, boosts performance on visual recognition tasks. Beyond the final layer, we apply the method at intermediate layers using an adaptive layer-matching mechanism trained via meta-optimization. Experiments on image classification and on transfer learning to visual recognition tasks indicate that the layer-wise variant consistently yields performance gains compared with state-of-the-art online KD approaches. These advantages show that the layer-wise variant can guide the network to produce better feature representations. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/winycg/L-MCL.

author: Daniel
title: Adversarial distillation without real-world data
abstract: In many real-world settings, alternative data or the original training data are usually unavailable, yet among existing KD algorithms, almost all are data-driven and rely on large quantities of such data. Knowledge Distillation (KD) has achieved remarkable progress over recent years and has become a popular paradigm for compressing models and transferring knowledge. We address this challenge by presenting a novel adversarial distillation mechanism that builds a compact student model without any real-world data. Central to the method, we define a model discrepancy that quantificationally measures the difference between student and teacher models, and we construct an optimizable upper bound for it. Within this framework, the student and the teacher jointly serve as the discriminator to reduce this discrepancy, whereas a generator adversarially produces "hard samples" to increase it. Across extensive experiments, the proposed data-free method attains performance comparable to existing data-driven methods. Even more notably, the approach can be directly extended to semantic segmentation, a problem more complicated than classification, where it achieves state-of-the-art results. Code and pretrained models are released at https://github.com/VainF/Data-Free-Adversarial-Distillation.

author: Martin
title: Applying knowledge distillation from BERT to seq2seq ASR
abstract: Attention-based sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) models have yielded promising results for automatic speech recognition (ASR), but because decoding proceeds left-to-right, right context is unavailable. We exploit both left and right context by using BERT as an external language model for seq2seq ASR via knowledge distillation. In the proposed method, BERT produces soft labels that supervise training of the seq2seq model. We additionally supply BERT with context outside the current utterance as input. Experimental evaluations on the Corpus of Spontaneous Japanese (CSJ) show significant gains over a seq2seq baseline. Distillation from BERT outperforms distillation from a transformer LM that only uses left context. We also confirm the effectiveness of leveraging context outside the current utterance. Compared with LM application strategies such as n-best rescoring and shallow fusion, the method attains better ASR performance without any extra inference cost.

author: Gray
title: Enhancing feature distillation using an ensemble of projectors
abstract: Research on knowledge distillation for features has largely emphasized loss function design and deciding which layers are distilled, whereas the influence of the feature projector that connects the teacher and the student has been comparatively overlooked. We first examine a plausible mechanism for the projector, supported by empirical evidence, and then introduce a feature distillation approach that employs an ensemble of projectors to further improve performance. We find that a student benefits from a projector even when the feature dimensions of the student and the teacher are identical. Training a student backbone without a projector can be viewed as multi-task learning: it must simultaneously learn discriminative feature extraction for classification and perform feature matching to the teacher for distillation. We hypothesize—and verify empirically—that in the absence of a projector, the student network tends to overfit the teacher’s feature distributions despite differences in architecture and weights initialization, degrading the quality of the student’s deep features that are ultimately used for classification. In contrast, inserting a projector disentangles these two learning objectives and allows the student network to concentrate on the main feature extraction task while still leveraging teacher features as guidance through the projector. Motivated by this positive role of the projector in feature distillation, we adopt an ensemble of projectors to further enhance the quality of student features. Experimental results on different datasets with a series of teacher–student pairs illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

author: Mayo
title: Soft Labels in Knowledge Distillation Viewed Through the Bias–Variance Tradeoff
abstract: Knowledge distillation uses a teacher—either a single well-trained network or an ensemble—to steer the training of a student network via the teacher’s outputs treated as soft labels. Prior work has shown that softening labels provides effective regularization for the student. From the standpoint of statistical learning, regularization primarily reduces variance, yet how bias and variance evolve under training with soft labels has remained unclear. We analyze the bias–variance tradeoff induced by distillation with soft labels and find that this tradeoff exhibits sample-wise variation during training. Moreover, for a fixed distillation temperature, we observe that distillation performance is negatively associated with the number of specific samples, which we call regularization samples because they increase bias while decreasing variance. However, we also empirically find that eliminating all regularization samples degrades distillation performance. These observations motivate a method that assigns weights to soft labels so that the network can adaptively manage the sample-wise bias–variance tradeoff. Experiments on standard evaluation benchmarks validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. Our code is available at https://github.com/bellymonster/Weighted-Soft-Label-Distillation.

author: Bowman
title: Compact universal paralinguistic speech representations via distillation
abstract: On-device use of state-of-the-art embedding models has been hampered by scarce public releases and heavy resource demands. At the same time, self-supervision has recently yielded markedly stronger speech representations. To address both, we publicly release a suite of paralinguistic speech models that are compact yet near state of the art. The proposed method relies on knowledge distillation, with models trained solely on public data. We vary architectures and conduct extensive evaluation on the Non-Semantic Speech (NOSS) benchmark. The largest distilled model is under 15% the size of the original model (314MB vs 2.2GB), attains over 96% the accuracy on 6 of 7 tasks, and is trained on 6.5% the data. The smallest variant occupies 1% of the size (22MB) while reaching over 90% the accuracy on 6 of 7 tasks. Our models outperform the open source Wav2Vec 2.0 model on 6 of 7 tasks, and the smallest model outperforms the open source Wav2Vec 2.0 on both emotion recognition tasks despite being 7% the size.

author: Hawkins
title: Accelerating Knowledge Distillation for Visual Recognition
abstract: Knowledge Distillation (KD) is widely used in visual applications, including supervised classification as well as representation learning in the self-supervised setting, but a vanilla KD pipeline expends most computation on forward passes through giant teacher networks, rendering training inefficient and costly. ReLabel, a recent alternative, constructs a label map for each full image; during training, a crop obtains its region-level label by RoI align from this precomputed global map, enabling efficient supervision generation without repeatedly invoking the teachers. However, because the KD teachers come from conventional multi-crop training, this strategy introduces mismatches between the global label map and region-level labels, which leads to performance deterioration. We present the proposed method, which reproduces the distillation training phase and produces soft labels within the multi-crop KD scheme, while training faster than ReLabel by eliminating post-processing such as RoI align and softmax. When multiple crops from the same image are loaded jointly, the proposed method is even more efficient than a conventional image classification framework. On ImageNet-1K, ResNet-50 attains 79.8%, outperforming ReLabel by approximately 1.0% while also running faster. On the self-supervised learning task, we also show that the proposed method has an efficiency advantage. Project page: http://zhiqiangshen.com/projects/FKD/index.html, and source code with models: https://github.com/szq0214/FKD.

author: Cohen
title: Attention-guided combinatorial fusion of teacher layers for knowledge distillation
abstract: Knowledge distillation is used as a strategy for training and compression in which two neural networks (a teacher and a student) are optimized jointly during training, the teacher acting as a dependable predictor and the student attempting to match its predictions. A smaller student architecture is typically chosen to obtain compression while still delivering high-quality results. In most configurations, only the final predictions are distilled, although the student could also benefit from the teacher’s supervision on internal components. We therefore investigate distillation at intermediate layers. Because student and teacher frequently lack a one-to-one alignment across layers, many existing techniques omit some teacher layers and distill from only a subset, and this shortcoming directly affects quality. To remedy this, the proposed method adopts a combinatorial scheme that relies on attention: it aggregates information on the teacher side, takes each layer’s significance into account, and then performs distillation between the resulting combination of teacher layers and the student’s layers. We apply this technique to distill BERT with 12 layers (Devlin et al. 2019) into counterparts with 6, 4, and 2 layers, and we evaluate them on GLUE tasks (Wang et al. 2018). Experimental results show that this combinatorial approach is able to outperform other existing techniques.

author: Cameron
title: Pre-training Matters for Compact Models: Evidence from Small Architectures
abstract: Advances in natural language representations have relied on very large, costly models that exploit self-supervised pre-training on massive general-domain corpora. Because applying such models to down-stream tasks is expensive, prior work has introduced multiple model compression methods for pre-trained language representations (Sun et al., 2019; Sanh, 2019). Yet the straightforward baseline of pre-training compact architectures and then fine-tuning them has, surprisingly, received little attention.
