We begin by demonstrating that, for smaller architectures, self-supervised pre-training still matters, and that fine-tuning pre-trained compact models can be competitive with more elaborate approaches proposed in concurrent work. Building on pre-trained compact models, we next investigate transferring task knowledge from large, fine-tuned models via standard knowledge distillation. This yields a simple, effective, and general algorithm—the proposed method—that brings further improvements. Through extensive experiments, we more broadly study how pre-training and distillation interact under two under-studied variables: model size and the properties of unlabeled task data. A surprising finding is that their effects compound even when the two are applied sequentially to the same data. To accelerate future research, we will release 24 pre-trained miniature BERT models to the public.

author: Parsons
title: Distilling Dense Retrieval with Curriculum Learning
abstract: Recent studies indicate that, by distilling ranking knowledge from a base re-ranking model that already exists, one can obtain more effective dense retrieval models. We introduce a generic optimization framework based on curriculum learning that adjusts the difficulty of training data generated by the re-ranking (teacher) model. The proposed method iteratively optimizes the dense retrieval (student) model by steadily increasing the difficulty of the knowledge distillation data it receives. Concretely, the student is first exposed to coarse-grained preference pairs between documents taken from the teacher's ranking, and is later required to satisfy finer-grained pairwise document ordering requirements. We implement a simple instance of this framework to enhance two state-of-the-art dense retrieval models. On three public passage retrieval datasets, results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework.

author: Perez
title: A distillation-based approach to multi-task Natural Language Understanding
abstract: Training multi-task neural networks to outperform—or even just match—single-task counterparts is often difficult. We address this using knowledge distillation in which single-task models serve as teachers for a multi-task model. To further improve training, we introduce a novel method that progressively shifts training from distillation toward supervised learning, which helps the multi-task model to surpass single-task teachers. Evaluation uses BERT multi-task fine-tuning on the GLUE benchmark. The proposed method consistently improves upon standard single-task and multi-task training.

author: Stewart
title: Knowledge Distillation for Privacy-Preserving Compression of Deep Neural Networks
abstract: Intelligent mobile applications increasingly require deploying powerful deep neural networks (DNNs) on mobile devices, yet the high accuracy of DNNs typically depends on ever more complex models whose computational expense exceeds the capacity of such devices. In addition, to build these sophisticated DNN models, app service providers must collect and use large volumes of users' data containing sensitive information, and direct deployment of these models to public mobile devices presents prohibitive privacy risk. To realize on-device deep learning without incurring capacity and privacy concerns, we design a private model compression framework, referred to here as the proposed method. Within the knowledge distillation paradigm, training of a compact and fast neural network jointly leverages hint learning, distillation learning, and self learning. The knowledge distilled from the cumbersome model is adaptively bounded and carefully perturbed to enforce differential privacy. We also introduce an elegant method for query sample selection to reduce the number of queries and control the privacy loss. A series of empirical evaluations, together with an implementation on an Android mobile device, indicate that the proposed method both compresses cumbersome models efficiently and provides a strong privacy guarantee. For example, on SVHN, under a meaningful (9.83,10^{-6})-differential privacy guarantee, the compact model produced by the proposed method achieves a 20× compression ratio and a 19× speed-up with only 0.97% accuracy loss.

author: Adams
title: On the purported incompatibility between label smoothing and knowledge distillation: an empirical analysis
abstract: We empirically examine the recent perspective that label smoothing and knowledge distillation are incompatible. We first explain why this claim emerges: label smoothing erases relative information among teacher logits. We then present a novel connection characterizing how label smoothing shapes the distributions for classes that are semantically similar versus dissimilar. Next, we introduce a metric that quantitatively measures the degree to which information is erased within a sample's representation. Building on this, we probe the one-sidedness and imperfection of this incompatibility view through massive analyses, visualizations, and comprehensive experiments across Neural Machine Translation, Image Classification, and Binary Networks. Lastly, we broadly discuss several circumstances where label smoothing indeed becomes ineffective. Project page: http://zhiqiangshen.com/projects/LS_and_KD/index.html.

author: Clark
title: On achieving model-agnostic federated learning through knowledge distillation
abstract: Can a universal API enable federated learning for an ad‑hoc collection of agents (data-holders) to collaborate? Such an interface must be model-agnostic, making no assumptions about the agents’ model architectures, and it also cannot depend on access to representative public data. Knowledge distillation (KD) appears to be the natural mechanism for building such protocols. Perhaps surprisingly, we demonstrate that most straightforward KD-based federated learning protocols perform poorly. To understand why, we introduce a new theoretical framework built on kernel ridge regression in the federated setting, which accounts for both model heterogeneity and data heterogeneity. Our analysis indicates that the observed degradation is largely driven by a fundamental limitation of knowledge distillation under data heterogeneity. We further substantiate this framework by analyzing and designing new KD-based protocols. In real-world experiments with neural networks, their performance, while still unsatisfactory, aligns closely with our theoretical predictions.

author: Hahn
title: A general framework for object detector distillation using Pearson Correlation Coefficient
abstract: In object detection, knowledge distillation (KD) is commonly adopted to train compact models, yet guidance on heterogeneous student-teacher pairs remains limited. We empirically observe that stronger FPN features from a heterogeneous teacher detector can help the student even when detection heads and label assignments differ. Simply forcing feature maps to match during distillation exposes two issues. First, differences in feature magnitude between teacher and student could impose overly strict constraints on the student. Second, FPN stages and channels with large feature magnitude in the teacher could dominate the gradient of distillation loss, which will overwhelm the effects of other features in KD and introduce much noise. To cope with these issues, the proposed method imitates features using Pearson Correlation Coefficient, emphasizing relational information from the teacher while relaxing constraints on feature magnitude. Across experiments, it consistently outperforms existing detection KD methods, is effective for homogeneous and heterogeneous student-teacher pairs alike, and also shows faster convergence. With a powerful MaskRCNN-Swin detector serving as teacher, ResNet-50 based RetinaNet and FCOS reach 41.5% and 43.9% mAP on COCO2017, respectively, representing gains of 4.1% and 4.8% over the baseline.

author: Walter
title: Knowledge distillation when the teacher is stronger
abstract: Most existing knowledge distillation studies address baseline settings in which the teacher models and training strategies are not as strong or as competitive as state-of-the-art approaches; in contrast, this paper introduces the proposed method to distill better from a stronger teacher. From empirical observation, the predictions from the student and from a stronger teacher may tend to diverge much more severely. Therefore, forcing exact agreement of predictions through KL divergence would disturb training and make existing methods perform poorly. We show that merely keeping the relations of the predictions from the teacher and the student would suffice, and we propose a correlation-based loss that explicitly captures the teacher’s intrinsic inter-class relations. Moreover, because different instances exhibit different semantic similarities to each class, we also apply this relational alignment within each class (the intra-class level). The proposed method is simple yet practical, and extensive experiments indicate that it adapts well across various architectures, model sizes, and training strategies, and can consistently achieve state-of-the-art performance on the tasks of image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation. Code is provided at https://github.com/hunto/DIST_KD.

author: Edwards
title: Privacy-Preserving Federated Learning via a Quantized Noisy Ensemble for One-Shot Offline Cross-Domain Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Across tasks in image and text classification, extensive experiments indicate that a privacy-preserving approach surpasses baseline FL algorithms on both accuracy and communication efficiency. We consider Federated Learning (FL), in which local nodes jointly train a central model while keeping training data decentralized. Prior FL strategies typically share model parameters or apply co-distillation to mitigate unbalanced data distribution, but they encounter communication bottlenecks and, more importantly, risks of privacy leakage. Within this setting, we introduce a privacy-preserving and communication-efficient method that performs one-shot, offline knowledge distillation using unlabeled public data from cross-domain sources. The approach aggregates an ensemble of local predictions—made by local models trained to completion—that is quantized and noisy, yielding stronger privacy guarantees while maintaining accuracy.

author: Rios
title: Enhancing Neural Topic Models via Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Analysts frequently rely on topic models to extract human-interpretable topics that elucidate large document collections. The proposed method employs knowledge distillation to integrate the strengths of probabilistic topic models and pretrained transformers. Owing to its modular design, it can be applied to any neural topic model, improving topic quality; we validate this on two models with disparate architectures and achieve state-of-the-art topic coherence. We further find that the adaptable framework yields gains not only when performance is aggregated across all estimated topics, as is commonly reported, but also in head-to-head comparisons between aligned topics.

author: Foster
title: Click-through rate prediction via knowledge distillation with an ensemble of teachers
abstract: Deep learning-based approaches for click-through rate (CTR) prediction are widely studied and have improved prediction accuracy in many industrial applications. However, much recent work primarily builds complex network architectures to better capture sophisticated feature interactions and dynamic user behaviors. The resulting model complexity may slow online inference and hinder adoption in real-time applications. We instead adopt a training strategy based on knowledge distillation (KD). KD uses a teacher–student learning setup in which knowledge from the teacher model is transferred to the student model. This strategy allows us to keep the student as a vanilla DNN model, while achieving significant accuracy improvements over state-of-the-art teacher models. These benefits motivate employing a powerful ensemble of teachers to train the student more accurately. We further propose techniques for ensemble-based CTR prediction, including teacher gating and early stopping by distillation loss. We conduct comprehensive experiments against 12 existing models across three industrial datasets. Both offline evaluations and online A/B testing show the effectiveness of our KD-based training strategy.

author: Rocha
title: Few-Shot Network Compression with Layer-wise Teacher-Student Distillation
abstract: Compressing models is widely used to build light-weighted deep neural networks. However, prevailing approaches usually require fine-tuning with sufficient training data to maintain accuracy, which can be constrained by privacy and security considerations. As a compromise between privacy and performance, we study few shot network compression: with only a few samples per class, how can a network be compressed with negligible performance drop? A key obstacle is high estimation errors from the original network at inference, because the compressed network can over-fits easily on the few training instances. These errors may propagate and accumulate in a layer-wise fashion and ultimately deteriorate the network output. To mitigate this, we present the proposed method, a novel layer-wise knowledge distillation procedure. By interleaving the teacher and student networks' hidden layers, the estimation errors accumulated layer-wisely are effectively reduced. The resulting approach forms a general framework that is compatible with prevalent network compression techniques, including pruning. On benchmark datasets, extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed method can significantly improve the student network's accuracy under the constraint of only a few training instances.

author: Ellis
title: Representation-focused knowledge distillation for graph neural networks
abstract: In knowledge distillation, resource-efficient graph neural networks (GNNs) are improved by guidance from more expressive but cumbersome teacher models. Prior work on distillation for GNNs introduced the Local Structure Preserving loss (LSP), which enforces agreement on local structural relationships defined on edges between the student and the teacher's node embeddings. We investigate whether emphasizing the global topology induced by the teacher's embedding of graph data constitutes a more effective distillation objective for GNNs, since real-world graphs frequently include latent interactions and noisy edges. We present the proposed method, which employs contrastive learning, implicitly maintaining global topology by aligning student node embeddings with those of the teacher within a shared representation space. We further broaden benchmarking with large-scale real-world datasets for which teacher–student GNN performance gaps are non-negligible. Across 14 heterogeneous GNN architectures and 4 datasets, experiments show that the proposed method consistently improves the performance and robustness of lightweight GNNs, outperforming LSP (and a variant of LSP that preserves global structure) and baselines from 2D computer vision. An analysis of representational similarity between teacher and student embedding spaces shows that the proposed method achieves a balance in preserving local and global relationships, whereas structure preserving approaches are most effective at preserving one rather than both. Our code is available at https://github.com/chaitjo/efficient-gnns

author: Baker
title: Reviving Low-Frequency Words in Non-Autoregressive Translation: Exploiting Authentic and Synthetic Parallel Data with Pretraining and Reverse Distillation
abstract: In training non-autoregressive translation (NAT) models, knowledge distillation (KD) is routinely used to create synthetic data. Yet a mismatch on low-frequency words between distilled and original data increases errors when predicting low-frequency words. To address this issue, we leverage pretraining so that NAT has direct access to the raw data. An analysis of directed alignments reveals that KD makes alignments from low-frequency source words to targets more deterministic, but it does not align enough low-frequency words from target to source. Motivated by this observation, we introduce reverse KD to recover additional alignments for low-frequency target words. To exploit both authentic and synthetic data, we integrate these complementary techniques into a new training strategy that further improves NAT performance. We evaluate on five translation benchmarks with two advanced architectures. Results demonstrate that the proposed approach can deliver significant and universal improvements in translation quality by cutting translation errors on low-frequency words. Encouragingly, the method attains 28.2 and 33.9 BLEU on WMT14 English-German and WMT16 Romanian-English, respectively. Code, data, and trained models are available at https://github.com/alphadl/RLFW-NAT.

author: Wright
title: Learning semantics with distillation for holistic scene understanding in videos
abstract: Autonomous systems require comprehensive knowledge of their surroundings. Recent work has shown that deep neural networks can learn geometry (depth) and motion (optical flow) from a monocular video without explicit ground truth supervision, and ground truth for these two tasks is particularly hard to source. We push holistic scene understanding with monocular cameras further by learning depth and motion together with semantics; for semantics, supervision comes from a pre-trained network that distills proxy ground truth images. The three tasks are handled jointly through (a) a new training protocol based on knowledge distillation and self-supervision and (b) a compact network architecture that makes scene understanding efficient on both power hungry GPUs and low-power embedded platforms. We conduct a thorough evaluation of the framework and demonstrate state-of-the-art results for monocular depth estimation, optical flow, and motion segmentation.

author: Hoffman
title: Knowledge Distillation for Federated Learning
abstract: Rather than disclosing raw data, many distributed learning frameworks share model parameters across workers. A representative case in point is federated learning, which communicates the gradients or weights of each neural network model. When bandwidth is constrained, this strategy can be prohibitively expensive, especially with modern deep neural networks that contain a very large number of model parameters. In contrast, federated distillation (FD) limits communication to only model outputs, whose dimensionality is commonly far smaller than the model size (e.g., MNIST has 10 labels). This chapter aims to provide a thorough account of FD, emphasizing both its communication efficiency and its applicability to a range of tasks. To clarify the mechanism underlying FD, the chapter first presents a novel asymptotic analysis of two foundational FD algorithms—knowledge distillation (KD) and co-distillation (CD)—using the neural tangent kernel (NTK) theory. The second part then describes a baseline FD implementation for a classification task and reports performance in terms of accuracy and communication efficiency, compared to FL. Finally, to illustrate how FD applies across diverse distributed learning tasks and environments, the third part covers two selected applications: FD over asymmetric uplink-and-downlink wireless channels and FD for reinforcement learning.

author: Baker
title: Distilling a Unified Classifier from Models with Diverse Architectures and Target Classes
abstract: We investigate forming a single classifier from a collection of classifiers that vary in architecture and in their target classes, when only a generic pool of unlabelled data is available. The setting arises in practice when data originate from multiple sources that cannot exchange raw data—for example because of privacy—and only models trained locally may be shared. Further, individual sources may lack data for some classes and may also be unable to train the same classification model owing to heterogeneous computational resources. To address this, the proposed method generalises knowledge distillation to merge such heterogeneous classifiers. We derive a probabilistic relationship linking the outputs of these classifiers to the probability over all classes. Leveraging this relation, we introduce two classes of methods, one based on cross-entropy minimisation and the other on matrix factorisation, which estimate soft labels covering all classes computed from unlabelled samples and use them in place of ground truth labels to train a unified classifier. Experimental results on the ImageNet, LSUN, and Places365 benchmarks show that these approaches significantly outperform a naive extension of knowledge distillation and can reach accuracy that is almost the same as that of classifiers trained in a centralised, supervised manner.

author: Richards
title: Text generation via knowledge distillation in generative adversarial networks
abstract: Many NLP applications rely on text generation, including language modeling, text summarization, and machine translation. In computer vision, GANs have achieved notable success for high-quality image generation, and interest in applying GANs to NLP has grown recently. Realizing comparable gains in NLP is harder because text is discrete. We present the proposed method, which uses knowledge distillation to more effectively leverage the GAN framework for text generation. We show that autoencoders (AEs) can yield a continuous representation of sentences that is smooth and assigns positive probability to multiple words. We distill this representation so the generator learns to produce similar smooth representations. We conduct experiments on different datasets to validate this idea and show that the proposed approach attains better performance, measured by BLEU and Jensen-Shannon distance (JSD), than traditional GAN-based text generation approaches without pre-training.

author: Hurst
title: A Distillation Approach for Learning Compact, High-Performance Ranking Models in Recommender Systems
abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has been shown in image recognition to deliver both effectiveness and efficiency. Building on KD, we present a new learning to rank approach (the proposed method) for applications such as recommender systems, aimed at being both effective and efficient. In this setup, a smaller student model is trained to rank documents/items using the original training data together with supervision from a larger teacher model. While the student attains ranking performance similar to the large teacher model's ranking performance, its reduced model size makes online inference more efficient. The proposed method is flexible: it is orthogonal to the particular ranking models chosen for teacher and student. We articulate and address the challenges that arise when using this approach for ranking problems. Experiments on public datasets and state-of-the-art models for recommendation indicate that the approach meets its intended goals: a student learned with the proposed method has less than half the size of the teacher model yet achieves ranking performance similar to the teacher and much better than a student learned without the proposed method.

author: Ross
title: Distilling Ensembles for Neural Machine Translation
abstract: Neural Machine Translation (NMT) decoding at the sentence level is time expensive, and smaller models reduce this cost. Knowledge distillation refers to training a student network to perform better by using a stronger teacher network for supervision. We show that the translation quality from an ensemble and from an oracle BLEU teacher network can be transferred into a single NMT system. We also report translation improvements when the teacher network shares the same architecture and dimensions as the student network. Because training the student model remains expensive, we introduce a data filtering method that uses the knowledge of the teacher model and both accelerates training and yields better translation quality. These techniques require no code changes and can be easily replicated on any NMT architecture to increase decoding speed.

author: Robinson
title: Diagnosing and Mitigating Lexical Choice Issues in Non-Autoregressive Translation
abstract: To train non-autoregressive translation (NAT) models, knowledge distillation (KD) with an autoregressive teacher model is commonly used to reduce the complexity of the raw data. We empirically show a side effect of this training: errors in lexical choice for low-frequency words are propagated from the teacher model into the NAT model. To alleviate this problem, the proposed method gives NAT models direct access to the raw data so that useful information about low-frequency words, absent from the distilled data, can be recovered. Concretely, we add an extra Kullback-Leibler divergence term that contrasts the NAT model's lexical choice against the lexical choice encoded in the raw data. Experiments over multiple language pairs and model architectures demonstrate both effectiveness and universality of the proposed method. Extensive analyses confirm our claim that the gains stem from reducing errors in lexical choice for low-frequency words. Encouragingly, on WMT14 English-German and WMT16 Romanian-English, the proposed method pushes SOTA NAT performance up to 27.8 and 33.8 BLEU points, respectively. We will release the source code.

author: Bright
title: Practical lipreading through distillation and efficient models
abstract: Advances following the resurgence of neural networks have driven substantial gains in lipreading, with recent studies focusing on choosing optimal architectures and on generalization. Nevertheless, a clear mismatch remains between prevailing approaches and the constraints that matter for effective deployment in practical settings. We contribute several elements that substantially narrow this gap. Through a set of architectural modifications—most notably a head that applies depthwise separable temporal convolution—we cut computational cost to a fraction of that of the original model, which was already quite efficient. Using self-distillation, we lift state-of-the-art accuracy on LRW and LRW-1000 to 88.5% and 46.6%, respectively, representing a wide-margin improvement. We further find that knowledge distillation recovers accuracy in lightweight models very effectively. Taken together, these components yield a spectrum of models exposing different accuracy–efficiency trade-offs. In particular, our strongest lightweight configurations reach parity with the current state-of-the-art while reducing computational cost and number of parameters by 8.2x and 3.9x, respectively. We expect these results to support the use of lipreading systems in practical applications.

author: Hicks
title: Distillation for Domain Adaptation: Teaching Across Domains
abstract: In many practical settings, training and test distributions do not match, making domain adaptation essential. Nevertheless, most deep learning–based methods require simultaneous training with data from both source and target domains, which is unattractive when models must be adapted to a large number of domains or to domains that evolve over time (e.g., spam detection where attackers continually change tactics). To address this, we present the proposed method, an adaptation of Knowledge Distillation (Bucilua et al., 2006; Hinton et al., 2015) to domain adaptation. By leveraging multiple teachers’ domain-specific expertise together with inter-domain similarity, a student model attains state-of-the-art performance on a standard sentiment analysis benchmark for unsupervised domain adaptation with multiple sources. In contrast, when only a single teacher is available, domain similarity is an inadequate gauge of trustworthiness. We introduce a simple metric that shows good correlation with the teacher’s accuracy on the target domain. Using this metric to select high-confidence examples and incorporating them into training enables the student model to achieve state-of-the-art results in the single-source setting.

author: Williams
title: Zero-shot knowledge transfer via adversarial teacher–student belief alignment
abstract: In many modern deep learning applications, the data that trained the teacher is unavailable due to increasing dataset sizes and stricter privacy regulations. We study training a smaller student under guidance from a large teacher network in this zero-shot setting, and present the proposed method that trains a student to match teacher predictions without any data or metadata. The core idea is to learn an adversarial generator that actively searches for images on which agreement between student and teacher is poor; these generated images are then used to train the student. We also introduce a metric that quantifies how well teacher and student beliefs coincide near decision boundaries. Using this setup, the resulting student closely approximates the teacher on simple datasets such as SVHN. On CIFAR10, despite using no data, we surpass the state of the art in few-shot distillation with 100 images per class. By this metric, our zero-shot student matches the teacher significantly more than a counterpart distilled using real data with respect to the teacher. Code: https://github.com/polo5/ZeroShotKnowledgeTransfer

author: Rodriguez
title: Distilling Knowledge from Graph Neural Networks and Surpassing Them: An Effective Framework for Knowledge Distillation
abstract: We present a knowledge distillation framework that transfers the knowledge of any trained GNN (teacher model) into a well-designed student model. The student model is constructed from two simple prediction mechanisms—label propagation and feature transformation—and is implemented as a trainable combination of parameterized label propagation and feature transformation modules, thereby preserving, respectively, structure-based and feature-based prior knowledge while absorbing information from the teacher. Semi-supervised learning on graphs is an important problem in machine learning, and recent GNN-based classification methods have demonstrated superiority over traditional approaches such as label propagation; however, their sophisticated architectures yield complex prediction mechanisms that may not fully exploit valuable prior knowledge in the data (e.g., structurally correlated nodes tend to share a class). By distilling from GNN teachers, the learned student can benefit from both prior knowledge and the knowledge contained in GNN teachers, leading to more effective predictions, and its prediction process is more interpretable than that of GNNs. We evaluate on five public benchmark datasets and use seven GNN models—GCN, GAT, APPNP, SAGE, SGC, GCNII and GLP—as the teacher models. Experimental results show that the learned student model can consistently outperform its corresponding teacher model by 1.4% - 4.7% on average. Code and data are available at https://github.com/BUPT-GAMMA/CPF

author: Burton
title: Enabling efficient large-scale Transformer language representations via hardware-oriented block-structured pruning
abstract: We present an efficient Transformer-based large-scale language representation that applies block-structured pruning tailored for hardware efficiency. The pruning procedure is optimized by embedding reweighted group Lasso. This approach markedly reduces weight storage and computation while achieving high compression rates. Although pre-trained large-scale language models already deliver strong accuracy on many natural language processing tasks, their adoption is constrained by limited weight storage and computational speed on hardware platforms, particularly for edge computing. On the General Language Understanding Evaluation (GLUE) benchmark with BERT, RoBERTa, and DistilBERT, experiments obtain as much as 5.0x, with zero or minor accuracy degradation on certain task(s). The proposed method is orthogonal to compact pre-trained language models based on knowledge distillation, exemplified by DistilBERT: when applied on top of DistilBERT, it provides an additional 1.79x average compression rate with zero or minor accuracy degradation. These properties make the final compressed model suitable for deployment on resource-constrained edge devices.

author: Conner
title: Task-specific distillation from BERT into compact neural networks
abstract: In natural language processing, model depth and complexity have been steadily increasing, with deep language representation models such as BERT, ELMo, and GPT emblematic of this shift. This has encouraged the belief that earlier, shallower neural networks for language understanding are obsolete. Contrary to that view, we demonstrate that very simple, lightweight neural networks remain competitive even without changing the architecture, using external training data, or adding any additional input features. We propose distillation from BERT—a state-of-the-art language representation model—into a single-layer BiLSTM, along with a siamese variant for sentence-pair tasks. On multiple datasets spanning natural language inference, sentiment classification, and paraphrasing, we obtain results comparable with ELMo while using roughly 100 times fewer parameters, and only 15 times less inference time.

author: Henderson
title: Graph-free MLPs via distillation of GNN knowledge for inference
abstract: In graph machine learning, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are popular and attain great results on wide tasks of node classification. However, their industry use is hindered in practice by scalability issues rooted in data dependency: at inference, they require neighbor nodes several hops from the target node, and retrieving these neighbors burdens latency-constrained applications. Prior inference acceleration approaches such as pruning and quantization can expedite GNNs through fewer Multiplication-and-ACcumulation (MAC) operations, yet their gains are bounded because the data dependency persists. In contrast, multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) avoid any graph dependency and thus infer far faster than GNNs, although they are generally less accurate for node classification. We exploit this complementarity by combining GNNs and MLPs through knowledge distillation (KD). We show that using GNN KD can boost MLP performance by large margins. The distilled MLPs—the proposed method—retain no inference graph dependency. With competitive accuracy, the proposed method runs 146X-273X faster than GNNs and 14X-27X faster than other acceleration methods. In a production setting involving both transductive and inductive predictions across 7 datasets, its accuracies improve over stand-alone MLPs by 12.36% on average and match GNNs on 6/7 datasets. A comprehensive analysis characterizes when and why the proposed method can reach competitive accuracies to GNNs and points to it as a handy choice for latency-constrained applications.

author: Brown
title: A Unified Approach to Vision Transformer Compression
abstract: Vision transformers (ViTs) have seen rising adoption. Trained on massive data, they can deliver competitive performance while forgoing customized image operators like convolutions. Nevertheless, their computational overhead remains prohibitive, primarily due to stacking multi-head self-attention modules and related components. Compared with the extensive and successful body of work on compressing convolutional neural networks, research on Vision Transformer compression has only just emerged, and most existing efforts target one or two aspects of compression. We present the proposed method: a single ViT compression framework that integrates pruning, layer skipping, and knowledge distillation. It sets up an end-to-end, budget-constrained optimization that jointly learns model weights, layer-wise pruning ratios/masks, and skip configurations under a distillation loss. The resulting optimization is addressed using the primal-dual algorithm. On the ImageNet dataset, experiments with several ViT variants, such as DeiT and T2T-ViT backbones, indicate that the proposed method consistently outperforms recent competitors. As an example, DeiT-Tiny can be reduced to 50% of the original FLOPs with almost no loss in accuracy. Code is available online: https://github.com/VITA-Group/UVC.

author: James
title: Progressive Self-Distillation for Robust Cross-Modal Representations
abstract: CLIP’s vision-language objective largely overlooks the noisy many-to-many correspondences characteristic of web-harvested image captioning datasets, which in turn leads to compute and data inefficiency. To mitigate this, the proposed method adopts cross-modal contrastive learning augmented with progressive self-distillation and soft image-text alignments to learn robust representations from noisy data more efficiently. During training, at every minibatch the model distills its own knowledge to dynamically produce soft-alignment targets for a portion of images and captions, and then updates its parameters using those targets. Across 14 benchmark datasets, it consistently outperforms a CLIP counterpart in multiple evaluation settings—zero-shot classification, linear probe transfer, and image-text retrieval—while incurring no added computational cost. Using an ImageNet-based robustness test-bed, we observe improved effective robustness under natural distribution shifts relative to both ImageNet-trained models and CLIP itself. Finally, pretraining on datasets that differ in size by two orders of magnitude indicates that the improvements over CLIP tend to scale with the number of training examples.

author: Ferrell
title: Improving Supernet Training with Alpha-Divergence
abstract: Weight-sharing neural architecture search (NAS) is an effective way to automate the construction of efficient neural architectures by optimizing a supernet that contains the candidate architectures as sub-networks, with the supernet and sub-networks trained jointly. The success of this approach depends heavily on distillation from the teacher supernet to the student sub-networks. We find that the commonly used distillation divergence, i.e., KL divergence, may cause student sub-networks to over-estimate or under-estimate the uncertainty of the teacher supernet, which leads to inferior performance of the sub-networks. To address this, the proposed method employs a more general alpha-divergence and adapts the choice of divergence during training, simultaneously preventing both over-estimation and under-estimation of the uncertainty of the teacher model. We apply this alpha-divergence based supernet training to slimmable neural networks as well as weight-sharing NAS, and demonstrate significant improvements. The model family discovered by this approach outperforms prior-art models across a wide range of FLOPs regimes, including BigNAS, Once-for-All networks, and AttentiveNAS. On ImageNet, the top-1 accuracy reaches 80.0% while using only 444M FLOPs. We release code and pretrained models at https://github.com/facebookresearch/AlphaNet.

author: Rice
title: Generalizing fake media detection through a continual representation learned with distillation
abstract: Across recent decades, artificial intelligence research has progressed substantially, yet practice still leans heavily on fixed datasets and stationary environments. Continual learning is a growing area that investigates how AI systems can learn in sequence from a continuous flow of related data, akin to biological systems. In parallel, fake media—such as deepfakes and synthetic face images—has become important to current multimedia technologies. Recently, numerous methods have been proposed that detect deepfakes with high accuracy. Nevertheless, their dependence on fixed datasets and limited evaluation settings leads to substantial shortcomings. Accordingly, this work incorporates continuous learning into the learning dynamics of neural networks and emphasizes its potential to significantly increase data efficiency. We introduce the proposed method, which learns a continual representation via distillation and leverages Continual Learning (CL), Representation Learning (RL), and Knowledge Distillation (KD). It is built to carry out sequential domain adaptation on new deepfake and GAN-generated synthetic face datasets while effectively minimizing catastrophic forgetting in a teacher–student model setting. Extensive experiments from our study demonstrate that the method is efficient for domain adaptation to detect low-quality deepfake videos and GAN-generated images across several datasets, outperforming state-of-the-art baseline methods.

author: Maddox
title: BERT compression by many-to-many layer mapping using Earth Mover's Distance
abstract: Although pre-trained language models such as BERT perform strongly on diverse NLP tasks, their memory and computation demands hinder effective deployment on resource-constrained devices. We present a BERT distillation approach using many-to-many layer mapping, in which every intermediate student layer may learn from any intermediate teacher layers. Consequently, for different NLP tasks, the student can adaptively draw supervision from different teacher layers. To realize this, we compute Earth Mover's Distance to obtain the minimum cumulative cost required to transform knowledge from the teacher network to the student network, enabling effective matching under the many-to-many layer mapping. In addition, we introduce a cost attention mechanism that automatically learns the layer weights used in EMD, which is supposed to further improve the model's performance and to accelerate the convergence time. Extensive experiments on the GLUE benchmark demonstrate that the proposed method achieves competitive performance against strong competitors in terms of both accuracy and model compression.

author: Valencia
title: A Review of Methods to Compress Deep Learning Models for Text
abstract: Practical NLP systems in industry must fit tight constraints: compact model size, short response times, and low power usage. Recently, information retrieval (IR) and natural language processing (NLP) have advanced markedly due to deep learning, including Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs), Long Short-Term Memory (LSTMs) networks, and Transformer [120] based architectures such as Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) [24], Generative Pre-training Transformer (GPT-2) [94], Multi-task Deep Neural Network (MT-DNN) [73], Extra-Long Network (XLNet) [134], Text-to-text transfer transformer (T5) [95], T-NLG [98], and GShard [63]. However, these models are very large. This survey reviews six categories of techniques—Knowledge Distillation, Quantization, Pruning, Tensor Decomposition, Parameter Sharing, and Sub-quadratic Transformer based methods—for compressing such models so they can be deployed in real industry NLP projects. Because there is a pressing need to build applications with small, efficient models and because many papers have appeared in this area recently, we believe this survey assembles the plethora of work from the 'deep learning for NLP' community over the past few years into a coherent narrative.

author: Smith
title: Automated Search to Compress Generative Adversarial Networks
abstract: Demand for running GANs on mobile devices, for applications including image translation, enhancement, and editing, has recently raised interest in compressing Generative Adversarial Networks. Despite substantial progress on compressing other deep models, work on compressing GANs—most often the generators—remains at an early stage, and existing algorithms handle only particular GAN architectures and losses. Motivated by advances of AutoML in deep compression, we apply AutoML to GAN compression and present the proposed method. It begins from an efficient, tailored search space and, under specified computational resource constraints, conducts an end-to-end search for new efficient generators. The search is guided by the original GAN through knowledge distillation, thereby achieving compression. The framework is fully automatic, standalone—no trained discriminators are required—and broadly applicable to various GAN models. We evaluate it on two representative GAN tasks: image translation and super resolution. Without additional components, the method produces compressed models that are remarkably lightweight while being more competitive, and they largely outperform existing alternatives. Codes and pretrained models are released at https://github.com/TAMU-VITA/AGD.

author: Le
title: Reframing video–pose embeddings for recognizing Activities of Daily Living
abstract: Recognition of Activities of Daily Living (ADL) often hinges on subtle distinctions between visually similar classes, motivating extensive work that fuses RGB with 3D Poses. Because recent 3D ConvNets exhibit rigidity that prevents them from capturing subtle visual patterns across an action, this line of research has largely favored joint RGB–3D Poses strategies. However, in settings without appropriate sensors, estimating 3D Poses from an RGB stream is computationally expensive, which impedes deployment in real-world applications that require low latency. This raises a key question: how can 3D Poses be exploited most effectively for ADL? We introduce an extension of a pose driven attention mechanism from prior work and investigate two complementary routes: (i) transferring Pose knowledge into RGB via feature-level distillation, and (ii) imitating pose driven attention by means of attention-level distillation. These two components are ultimately combined into a single model (the proposed method). We demonstrate that the proposed method is effective and further delivers a high speed up together with high resilience to noisy Poses. On 4 public datasets, it surpasses the representative baselines both with and without 3D Poses. Code is available at https://github.com/srijandas07/vpnplusplus.

author: Maldonado
title: Knowledge Distillation via Feature Mimicking
abstract: In knowledge distillation (KD), a compact student is guided by a high-capacity teacher. Most prior approaches rely on the teacher’s soft logits to provide additional supervision for the student. We contend it is more beneficial to require the student to mimic teacher features at the penultimate layer. This lets the student directly learn more effective information from the teacher feature, and also makes feature mimicking applicable to teachers trained with no softmax layer. Experiments show that this strategy achieves higher accuracy than traditional KD. To further support feature mimicking, we decompose the feature vector into its magnitude and its direction. We argue that the teacher should allow more freedom to the student feature magnitude, while encouraging the student to focus on mimicking the feature direction. To satisfy this, the proposed method introduces a loss term built on locality-sensitive hashing (LSH). With this new loss, the proposed method indeed achieves more accurate feature direction mimicking, relaxes constraints on the feature magnitudes, and achieves state-of-the-art distillation accuracy. We provide theoretical analyses explaining how LSH facilitates feature direction mimicking, and we further extend feature mimicking to object detection and multi-label recognition.

author: Herrera
title: Reducing GAN parameter counts through knowledge distillation
abstract: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) are applied to synthetic data generation, super resolution, and domain transfer, yet contemporary GANs commonly contain on the order of tens of millions of parameters. This scale makes deployment costly on low-SWAP hardware (size, weight, and power), including mobile devices, and in settings with real time capabilities. We find no prior work that reduces the number of parameters used in GANs. We therefore propose compressing GANs with knowledge distillation: a smaller “student” GAN is trained to mimic a larger “teacher” GAN. On MNIST, CIFAR-10, and Celeb-A, the proposed distillation compresses teacher GANs by 1669:1, 58:1, and 87:1, respectively, while preserving the quality of generated images. Experiments indicate a qualitative limit to how far a GAN can be compressed. In addition, for a fixed parameter budget, compressed GANs outperform GANs trained with standard training methods. We conjecture that the optimization landscape of over-parameterized GANs, which enables efficient training via alternating gradient descent, partially explains these observations. Thus, training an over-parameterized GAN and then applying the proposed compression yields a high quality generative model with a small number of parameters.

author: Davidson
title: Robust Re-Identification via Teacher-Student Distillation from Diverse Views
abstract: Achieving robustness in Re-Identification commonly relies on exploiting tracking cues in a Video-To-Video setting. Nevertheless, with single image queries (the Image-To-Video case), such pipelines undergo a severe performance drop. Prior studies alleviate this by transferring temporal information from a Video-based network into an Image-based counterpart. We propose a training procedure that transfers a superior knowledge that originates from a collection of views of the same target. The proposed method treats the diversity of views as a supervision signal within a teacher-student framework: a teacher exposed to many views performs knowledge distillation to a student that observes fewer views. Consequently, the student surpasses both its teacher and the current state of the art for Image-To-Video, by a wide margin (6.3% mAP on MARS, 8.6% on Duke-Video-ReId, and 5% on VeRi-776). An extensive analysis on Person, Vehicle, and Animal Re-ID examines the properties of the proposed method from both qualitative and quantitative perspectives. Code is available at https://github.com/aimagelab/VKD.

author: Rodriguez
title: Publishing Graph Neural Networks under Differential Privacy Guarantees
abstract: As graph neural networks (GNNs) see growing use in sensitive areas such as healthcare and medicine, the privacy properties of trained GNNs have become a concern. In particular, they are susceptible to privacy attacks, including membership inference attacks, even when an adversary has only black-box queries to the trained model. We present a privacy-preserving approach for releasing GNN models in a centralized setting. Given a public unlabeled graph, the proposed method releases GNN models that are trained explicitly on public data while leveraging, in a privacy preserving manner, knowledge derived from the private data. It integrates the knowledge-distillation framework with two noise mechanisms—random subsampling and noisy labeling—to provide rigorous privacy guarantees. We provide a theoretical analysis within the Renyi differential privacy framework. Experiments demonstrate solid performance relative to several baselines adapted to graph-structured data. Code is available at https://github.com/iyempissy/privGnn.

author: Graham
title: Federated Learning with Architectural Regularization via Auxiliary Branches at Multiple Levels
abstract: We introduce a novel architectural regularization technique for federated learning that, inside each local model, constructs multiple auxiliary branches by grafting subnetworks from the local and the global models at several different levels. Within the local model, the main pathway is trained so that its representations are congruent with those of these auxiliary hybrid pathways through online knowledge distillation. This design directly targets the critical challenge that heterogeneity and imbalance in data across clients cause mismatches among local networks and destabilize convergence of global models. The proposed technique is effective in robustifying the global model even under a non-iid setting and applies conveniently to various federated learning frameworks without incurring extra communication costs. Comprehensive empirical studies indicate remarkable performance gains in both accuracy and efficiency over existing methods. Code is released on our project page.

author: Chavez
title: Compressing Deep Neural Networks Using Data-Free Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Recent progress in model compression has yielded ways to shrink large neural networks down to a small fraction of the original size, typically keeping most, and sometimes all, of their accuracy. Yet every such technique assumes the original training set is available—a requirement that can fail when the target network was trained on an extremely large corpus or on data that cannot be released for privacy or safety reasons, as in some biometrics applications. We introduce a data-free knowledge distillation procedure that reduces deep neural networks trained on large-scale datasets to a fraction of the original size using only additional metadata bundled with a pretrained model. We further investigate multiple forms of metadata compatible with the proposed method and analyze the tradeoffs associated with each.

author: Mckay
title: Towards Efficient Distillation of Large-scale Language Models with Mixup
abstract: Recent large-scale language models achieve strong empirical results, but these gains come with larger models, higher power consumption, and slower inference, limiting use on memory- and computation-constrained platforms. Knowledge distillation (KD) offers an effective framework for compressing such models. However, large-scale neural networks tend to memorize training instances and can make inconsistent predictions when the data distribution shifts slightly. Furthermore, when task-specific data are scarce, the student has few opportunities to obtain useful information from the teacher. To tackle these issues, the proposed method is a data-agnostic distillation framework that leverages mixup, a simple yet efficient data augmentation strategy, to strengthen the generalization ability of the resulting model. Concretely, besides the original training examples, the student is trained to mimic the teacher's behavior on linear interpolations formed from pairs of examples. From a theoretical perspective, under reasonable conditions, this design yields a smaller gap between the generalization error and the empirical error. We validate effectiveness on the GLUE benchmark, where the proposed method consistently delivers significant gains over standard KD training and outperforms several competitive baselines. Experiments in a limited-data setting and ablation studies further demonstrate the advantages of the proposed approach.

author: Liu
title: Turning CLIP into a multimodal generator through vision-language knowledge distillation
abstract: Large-scale vision-language pre-training (VLP) of dual-stream models such as CLIP on massive collections of image–text pairs has delivered superior results on a range of multimodal alignment tasks. Nevertheless, these models remain unable to perform multimodal generative tasks because the text encoder is weak. We address this by equipping the dual-stream VLP model with a textual pre-trained language model (PLM) using a vision-language knowledge distillation procedure, thereby enabling multimodal generation. Compared with pre-training from scratch, this distillation is pretty data- and computation-efficient. Experiments show strong zero-shot performance on multimodal generation tasks, including open-ended visual question answering and image captioning. For instance, the model attains 44.5% zero-shot accuracy on the VQAv2 dataset, surpassing the previous state-of-the-art zero-shot model with 7× fewer parameters. Furthermore, the original textual language understanding and generation ability of the PLM is maintained after distillation, which makes the model versatile for both multimodal and unimodal tasks.

author: Mason
title: Student Networks via Teacher Feature Embedding
abstract: Deep convolutional neural networks are pervasive across applications, yet their storage and computational resource demands hinder deployment on mobile devices. Within knowledge distillation, a portable student network is optimized by drawing knowledge from a well-trained heavy teacher network. Many teacher-student approaches historically insert additional fully-connected layers to link intermediate layers in the teacher and student networks, introducing many auxiliary parameters. Unlike these designs, the proposed method propagates information from teacher to student while introducing no new variables that must be optimized. We treat the teacher-student setting through the lens of feature embedding. By incorporating a locality preserving loss, the student network is driven to produce low-dimensional features that inherit intrinsic properties of their corresponding high-dimensional features from the teacher network. As a consequence, the portable network can naturally maintain the teacher network's performance. We provide theoretical analysis supporting the lower computation complexity of the proposed method. Results on benchmark datasets with well-trained networks indicate that the proposed algorithm is superior to state-of-the-art methods for teacher-student learning in terms of computational and storage complexity.

author: White
title: Knowledge distillation for portable Generative Adversarial Networks in image-to-image translation
abstract: Existing network compression methods concentrate on visual recognition tasks and have never addressed generation tasks. At the same time, although Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) are widely used for image-to-image translation, they are hardly applicable on mobile devices owing to heavy computation and storage cost. We adopt knowledge distillation to train a student generator with fewer parameters, which inherits low-level and high-level information from the original heavy teacher generator. To promote the capability of the student generator, we introduce a student discriminator that measures distances among real images and images generated by the student and teacher generators. This establishes an adversarial learning process to optimize the student generator and the student discriminator. Experiments on benchmark datasets, including both qualitative and quantitative analysis, demonstrate that the proposed method can learn generative models that are portable and achieve strong performance.

author: Gaines
title: Task-Adaptive Compression of BERT via Differentiable Neural Architecture Search
abstract: BERT and other large pre-trained language models are effective on many natural language processing tasks, but their huge parameter size limits deployment in real-time applications that demand quick inference under constrained resources. Prior compression approaches typically turn BERT into small models in a task-independent way, namely applying the same compressed BERT across different downstream tasks. To address the necessity and benefits of task-oriented BERT compression, the proposed method employs differentiable Neural Architecture Search to automatically derive task-adaptive small models from BERT for specific tasks. We add a task-oriented knowledge distillation loss to provide search hints and include an efficiency-aware loss as search constraints, enabling a good balance between efficiency and effectiveness for task-adaptive BERT compression. We evaluate the proposed method on several NLP tasks, and the results show that the resulting task-adaptive compressed models are 12.7x to 29.3x faster than BERT in inference time and 11.5x to 17.0x smaller in terms of parameter size, while comparable performance is maintained.

author: Harrell
title: Federated learning on heterogeneous devices with size-adaptive models that include all clients
abstract: Federated learning (FL) enables training a global model from decentralized data while preserving privacy. Most FL approaches typically presume that any participating client can host the global model for training. In practice, however, client devices are heterogeneous and differ markedly in computing power. Although large models such as BERT have achieved major success in AI, deploying them in heterogeneous FL that includes weak clients is difficult. Straightforward remedies—dropping weak clients or adopting a single small model for all clients—will result in several issues, such as under-representation of the removed clients and inferior accuracy arising from data loss or limited model representation ability. To address this, we propose the proposed method, a client-inclusive federated learning method. Its central principle is to match model size to client capability: larger models on powerful clients and smaller models on weak clients. We also describe an effective way to share knowledge among multiple local models with different sizes. With this design, all clients can participate in model learning under FL, and the final model can be large and sufficiently powerful. Besides, we introduce a momentum knowledge distillation method to better transfer knowledge from big models on powerful clients to the small models on weak clients. We conduct extensive experiments on numerous real-world benchmark datasets, which show that the proposed method effectively learns accurate models from clients with heterogeneous devices within the FL framework.

author: Evans
title: Training Small Evaluation Metrics for Machine Translation
abstract: Work on related tasks suggests that efficiency is greatest at large scale, thereby making evaluation costly and impractical. At the same time, advances for MT and multilingual text generation have prompted the adoption of trained metrics such as COMET and BLEURT that frame scoring as regression and draw on representations from multilingual pre-trained encoders like XLM-RoBERTa and mBERT. We study the balance between multilinguality and capacity with RemBERT on data from the WMT Metrics Shared Task. A set of experiments indicates that, indeed, cross-lingual transfer is bottlenecked by model size, and we then show that distillation can mitigate this limitation by leveraging synthetic data generation and by transferring knowledge from a single teacher into several student models covering related languages. The proposed method improves over vanilla fine-tuning by as much as 10.5% and reaches 92.6% of RemBERT's performance with only a third of its parameters.

author: Fowler
title: Distillation under self-supervision for visual representation
abstract: We study self-supervised learning when the target models are small. Our empirical studies indicate that the widely used contrastive self-supervised method, despite its strong progress in training large models, performs poorly with small models. To address this, we introduce the proposed method, a self-supervised distillation approach in which a larger network (Teacher) transfers representational knowledge to a smaller architecture (Student). Rather than learning directly from unlabeled data, the student encoder is trained to mimic the similarity score distribution that the teacher infers over a set of instances. This leads to dramatic gains for small networks on downstream tasks. Relative to self-supervised baselines, the proposed method raises top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1k from 42.2% to 67.6% for EfficientNet-B0 and from 36.3% to 68.2% for MobileNet-v3-Large.

author: Lynch
title: Sensor-based action recognition via cross-modal knowledge distillation from vision
abstract: Recent studies report that multi-modal human activity recognition (HAR) achieves higher accuracy, yet the limited compute on wearable devices such as smartwatches prevents direct deployment of such methods. We present an end-to-end framework that performs knowledge distillation from the vision modality to the sensor modality. At inference time, the wearable provides only time-series signals (accelerometer data), which both lowers the computational burden on edge devices and yields a student whose performance closely approaches that of a computationally expensive multi-modal model. To enable the use of visual deep learning models while preserving local temporal dependencies, the time-series are first transformed into two-dimensional images via a Gramian Angular Field (GAF) encoding. In our design, ResNet18 serves as the teacher and a multi-scale TRN with BN-Inception serves as the student. We also introduce a novel loss that addresses modality discrepancies between vision and sensor by enforcing distance- and angle-wise semantic knowledge. Extensive experiments on UTD-MHAD, MMAct, and Berkeley-MHAD demonstrate that the proposed method is effective and competitive and can be deployed on wearable sensors.

author: Hernandez
title: Efficient novel view synthesis via distillation from Neural Radiance Field to Neural Light Field
abstract: The rapid growth of work on Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) has revealed strong promise for representing complex scenes with neural networks, but its inference time is a major bottleneck: producing a single pixel typically entails on the order of hundreds of queries to the NeRF network. Most prior approaches try to cut down the number of sampled points, yet iterative sampling remains. By contrast, Neural Light Field (NeLF) offers a simpler route for novel view synthesis—one pixel can be computed with a single forward pass, without ray-marching. We employ a deep residual MLP (88 layers) to learn the light field effectively. We show that the key to successfully training such a deep NeLF is having sufficient data, which we obtain by transferring knowledge from a pre-trained NeRF via data distillation. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world scenes demonstrate the merits of the proposed method over counterpart algorithms. On synthetic scenes, we attain a 26–35x reduction in FLOPs (per camera ray) and a 28–31x runtime speedup, while delivering significantly better rendering quality than NeRF, with a 1.4–2.8 dB average PSNR improvement, and without any customized parallelism requirement.

author: Farmer
title: Improving Efficiency of 3D Object Detectors Using Knowledge Distillation
abstract: High-performing 3D detectors typically incur large computation costs. We therefore investigate knowledge distillation (KD) as a path to efficient 3D object detectors, with an emphasis on popular pillar- and voxel-based detectors. Because suitable teacher-student pairs are not readily available, we first identify student models that balance accuracy and efficiency through model compression and lowering input resolution. Using six carefully constructed teacher-student pairs, we then establish a benchmark that evaluates existing KD approaches originally developed for the 2D domain in the context of 3D object detection. Beyond this study, the proposed method introduces an improved KD pipeline combining: (i) an enhanced logit KD that applies distillation only at a small set of key positions selected by the teacher classification response, and (ii) a teacher-guided student initialization that transfers the teacher model's feature extraction ability to students via weight inheritance. Extensive experiments on the Waymo dataset support our conclusions. Our strongest model reaches 65.75% LEVEL 2 mAPH, exceeds its teacher, and uses only 44% of the teacher flops. Our fastest model attains 51 FPS on an NVIDIA A100, achieving 2.2× the speed of PointPillar while also delivering higher accuracy. Code is available at https://github.com/CVMI-Lab/SparseKD.

author: Ryan
title: Distilling knowledge from multi-modal segmentation networks into mono-modal segmentation networks
abstract: In routine clinical workflows, constraints on physician and scanner availability, together with the need to limit costs and scan time, usually make acquisition of multiple modalities infeasible; in practice, a single modality is most often obtained. Nevertheless, extensive recent work has examined joint use of multiple imaging modalities for medical image segmentation, and fusion across modalities has been shown to raise segmentation accuracy relative to mono-modal segmentations in several applications. To address this mismatch, we introduce the proposed method, which transfers knowledge from a trained multi-modal segmentation network (teacher) to a mono-modal one (student). It adapts the generalized distillation framework so that the student network is trained using a subset (1 modality) of the teacher’s inputs (n modalities). We demonstrate its effectiveness on brain tumor segmentation using the BraTS 2018 dataset. Using different architectures, we find that the student network learns effectively from the teacher and always outperforms the baseline mono-modal network in terms of segmentation accuracy.

author: Osborne
title: Knowledge Distillation from Deep Networks for the Healthcare Domain
abstract: The rapid expansion of Electronic Healthcare Records (EHR) is creating both opportunities and urgent requirements within Computational Phenotyping to identify meaningful data-driven representations and disease patterns. Although Deep Learning models deliver superior performance on robust prediction for computational phenotyping tasks, their model interpretability is limited, a concern that is crucial for clinicians engaged in decision-making. We present a novel knowledge-distillation approach (the proposed method) that learns interpretable phenotype features to enable robust prediction while mimicking deep learning models' performance. The framework employs Gradient Boosting Trees to learn interpretable features based on outputs from deep learning models, including Stacked Denoising Autoencoder as well as Long Short-Term Memory. An exhaustive evaluation on a real-world time-series clinical dataset shows that the proposed method achieves similar or better performance, compared with the deep learning models, and provides interpretable phenotypes to support clinical decision making.

author: Moreno
title: Enabling Perception-Aware, Agile Quadrotor Navigation in Cluttered Environments via Learning
abstract: Neural control policies have recently surpassed existing model-based planning-and-control methods on minimum-time autonomous quadrotor navigation in cluttered environments, yet they are not perception aware. Perception awareness is crucial in vision-based navigation because of the limited field of view of the camera and the underactuated nature of a quadrotor. We introduce a learning-based system that achieves perception-aware, agile flight in cluttered environments. The proposed method merges reinforcement learning (RL) and imitation learning within a privileged learning-by-cheating framework. With RL, we first obtain a perception-aware teacher policy that, using full-state information, flies through cluttered environments in minimum time. Next, imitation learning distills its knowledge into a vision-based student policy that perceives the environment only via a camera. By tightly coupling perception and control, the approach yields a significant advantage in computation speed (10 times faster) and in success rate. Closed-loop control performance is demonstrated using hardware-in-the-loop simulation.

author: Smith
title: A general approach to small, fast, and effective domain pre-trained language models
abstract: Across a wide range of natural language processing tasks, large pre-trained models have been highly successful. Yet, applying them to specific domains incurs domain shift and creates difficulties for fine-tuning and online serving under latency and capacity constraints. We introduce a general approach that yields pre-trained models for specific domains that are small, fast, and effective. It combines adaptation of off-the-shelf general pre-trained models with task-agnostic knowledge distillation in the target domains. During adaptation, we propose domain-specific vocabulary expansion and automatically determine the size of the incremental vocabulary using corpus level occurrence probability. We then carry out a systematic exploration of different compression strategies for large pre-trained models in specific domains. Experiments are conducted in the biomedical and computer science domain. On domain-specific tasks, the proposed method outperforms the BERT BASE model; relative to BERT BASE, it is 3.3x smaller and 5.1x faster. Code and pre-trained models can be found at https://aka.ms/adalm.

author: Nguyen
title: Training Compact Highway Deep Neural Networks via Knowledge Distillation
abstract: For embedded devices, deployability is hampered because neural network models are typically far larger than conventional Gaussian mixture acoustic models. At the same time, recent years have seen deep learning markedly raise the state of the art in speech recognition. As part of earlier work, we studied a compact HDNN (highway deep neural network) for acoustic modelling, a depth-gated feedforward neural network. Those HDNN-based acoustic models achieved recognition accuracy comparable to plain DNN acoustic models while using far fewer model parameters. Building on that, the proposed method applies knowledge distillation, also referred to as teacher-student training: the compact HDNN is trained under the supervision of a high accuracy cumbersome model. We additionally examine sequence training and adaptation within the teacher-student training setting. Experiments are conducted on the AMI meeting speech recognition corpus. Using this technique, we significantly improved recognition accuracy for an HDNN acoustic model with under 0.8 million parameters and reduced the difference to a plain DNN with 30 million parameters.
